chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: Our age is putting on ein wirklicher Ausverkauf — a genuine clearance sale — and not only in trade: in the realm of ideas too. Everything can be had at such a rock-bottom price that one begins to wonder whether in the end anyone will still want to bid. Every speculative billiard-marker who conscientiously keeps score of the momentous progress of modern philosophy, every private lecturer, tutor and student, every smallholder and lodger in philosophy, does not stop at doubting everything but goes further. It would perhaps be untimely and inopportune to ask them where they actually get to. But it is surely polite and modest to take it as settled that they have doubted everything; otherwise it would be a strange thing to say, that they went further. This preliminary movement, then, they have all made — and presumably so easily that they do not find it necessary to let fall a single word about how. For not even the person who anxiously and with concern looked for a little enlightenment found any: not a guiding hint, not a small dietary prescription for how one is to conduct oneself under this enormous task. “But surely Descartes did it?” Descartes, a venerable, humble and upright thinker whose writings no one, surely, can read without the deepest emotion, did as he said and said as he did. Alas! Alas! Alas! In our time that is a great rarity! Descartes, as he himself repeats often enough, did not doubt with regard to faith. (“Memores tamen, ut jam dictum est, huic lumini naturali tamdiu tantum esse credendum, quamdiu nihil contrarium a Deo ipso revelatur ..... Præter cætera autem, memoriæ nostræ pro summa regula est infigendum, ea quæ nobis a Deo revelata sunt, ut omnium certissima esse credenda; et quamvis forte lumen rationis, quam maxime clarum et evidens, aliud quid nobis suggerere videretur, soli tamen auctoritati divinæ potius quam proprio nostro judicio fidem esse adhibendam.” [Remembering, however, as has already been said, that this natural light is to be trusted only so long as nothing to the contrary is revealed by God himself ..... Above all, though, we must fix in our memory as the supreme rule that what God has revealed to us is to be believed as the most certain of all things; and even if perhaps the light of reason, however clear and evident, should seem to suggest something else to us, we must still put our faith in divine authority alone rather than in our own judgment.] Cf. Principia philosophiæ, part one, § 28 and § 76.) He did not cry “Fire!” and make it everyone’s duty to doubt; for Descartes was a quiet, solitary thinker, not a bellowing night watchman in the street. He modestly admitted that his method had significance only for himself, and that it arose in part from the muddle his earlier learning had been in. (“Ne quis igitur putet, me hic traditurum aliquam methodum, quam unusquisque sequi debeat ad recte regendam rationem; illam enim tantum, quam ipsemet secutus sum, exponere decrevi... Sed simul ac illud studiorum curriculum absolvi (sc. juventutis, quo decurso mos est in eruditorum numerum cooptari, plane aliud coepi cogitare. Tot enim me dubiis totque erroribus implicatum esse animadverti, ut omnes discendi conatus nihil aliud mihi profuisse judicarem, quam quod ignorantiam meam magis magisque detexissem.” [So let no one suppose that I mean to hand down here some method that everyone ought to follow in order to guide his reason rightly; for I have resolved to set out only the one I myself have followed... But as soon as I had finished that course of study (namely, of my youth), at the end of which it is the custom to be admitted to the ranks of the learned, I began to think something quite different. For I found myself entangled in so many doubts and so many errors that I judged that all my efforts to learn had done me no other good than to uncover my ignorance more and more.] Cf. Dissertatio de methodo, pp. 2 and 3.) — The ancient Greeks, who did after all know something about philosophy too, held doubting to be the task of a whole life, because the skill of doubting is not acquired in days or weeks. The old veteran who had served his time attained it: through every snare he had held doubt in equilibrium, had fearlessly denied the certainty of the senses and the certainty of thought, and had incorruptibly withstood the anxiety of self-love and the insinuations of fellow-feeling. What the Greeks took for a life’s task and the veteran attained — that is what everyone in our time begins with.

In our time nobody stops at faith; everyone goes further. To ask where they get to would perhaps be foolhardy. On the other hand, it is surely a sign of good manners and cultivation on my part that I assume everyone has faith, since otherwise it would be a strange thing to say: to go further. Back in those old days things were different: faith was then the task of a whole life, since people assumed that the skill of believing is acquired neither in days nor in weeks. When the tested old man drew near his end, having fought the good fight and kept the faith, then his heart was still young enough that he had not forgotten that anxiety and trembling which disciplined the youth — which the grown man did indeed master, but which no human being ever entirely outgrows, unless, that is, he manages it by going further as early as possible. Where those venerable figures arrived, that is where, in our time, everyone begins — in order to go further.

The present author is no philosopher whatsoever. He has not understood the System — whether there is one, whether it is finished. His weak head already has enough to cope with in the thought of what an enormous head everyone in our time must have, since everyone has such an enormous thought. Even if one were able to translate the whole content of faith into the form of the concept, it does not follow that one has comprehended faith — comprehended how one came into it, or how it came into oneself. The present author is no philosopher whatsoever. Poetice et eleganter (poetically and elegantly put), he is an extra clerk, one who writes neither the System nor promises of the System, and who neither makes a slip of the pen on the System nor signs himself away to the System. He writes because for him it is a luxury, one that gains in pleasantness and obviousness the fewer people buy and read what he writes. He easily foresees his fate in an age that has struck a line through passion in order to serve scholarship — an age in which an author who wants readers must take care to write in such a way that it can be comfortably leafed through during the after-dinner nap, and take care to model his outward manner on that polite gardener’s boy in the Adresseavis who, hat in hand and with good references from his last place, recommends himself to a highly esteemed public. He foresees his fate: to be completely ignored. He has a presentiment of the terrible thing, that the zealous critics will make him run the gauntlet more than once. He dreads the still more terrible thing, that some enterprising abstractor or other, a gobbler of paragraphs (who, to save scholarship, is always willing to do to other people’s writings what Trop, “to save taste,” magnanimously did to “The Destruction of the Human Race”) — will cut him up into §§, and do it with the same inflexibility as the man who, to serve the science of punctuation, divided up his speech by counting the words, so that there were 50 words to a full stop and 35 to a semicolon. — I prostrate myself in deepest submission before every systematic customs-snooper: “This is not the System; it has not the slightest thing to do with the System. I call down all good things upon the System and upon the Danish partners in this omnibus, for a tower it is hardly likely to become. To each and every one of them, jointly and severally, I wish good luck and blessing.”
Most respectfully, Johannes de silentio.

chapters.title: Attunement
paragraphs: There was once a man who had heard, as a child, that beautiful story of how God tempted Abraham, and how Abraham stood firm in the temptation, kept the faith, and, against all expectation, received a son a second time. As he grew older, he read that same story with even greater admiration; for life had separated what had been united in the child’s pious simplicity. The older he grew, the more often his thoughts turned to that story. His enthusiasm grew stronger and stronger, and yet he could understand the story less and less. At last he forgot everything else over it. His soul had only one wish — to see Abraham — and only one longing: to have been a witness to that event. What he craved was not to see the fair lands of the East, nor the earthly splendor of the land of promise, nor that God-fearing married couple whose old age God blessed, nor the patriarch’s venerable figure, full of years, nor the lush youth of Isaac, the gift of God — he would not have minded if the same thing had taken place on a barren heath. What he yearned for was to go along on the three-day journey on which Abraham rode with sorrow before him and Isaac at his side. His wish was to be there in the hour when Abraham raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah far off, the hour when he left the donkeys behind and went up the mountain alone with Isaac; for what absorbed him was not the imagination’s artful weaving but the shudder of thought.

That man was not a thinker. He felt no need to get beyond faith. To him it seemed that it must be the most glorious thing of all to be remembered as its father, and an enviable lot to possess it, even if no one knew.
That man was not a learned exegete; he did not know Hebrew. Had he known Hebrew, perhaps he would easily have understood the story of Abraham.
“And God tempted Abraham, and said to him: Take Isaac, your only son, the one you love, and go into the land of Moriah, and there sacrifice him as a burnt offering on a mountain I will show you.”

It was early morning. Abraham rose early, had the donkeys saddled and left his tent, taking Isaac with him; but from the window Sarah followed them with her eyes, down through the valley, until she could no longer see them. For three days they rode in silence. On the morning of the fourth day Abraham said not a single word, but raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah far off. He left the young servants behind and, with Isaac by the hand, went up the mountain alone. But Abraham said to himself: “Still, I will not hide from Isaac where this road is leading him.” He stopped and laid his hand on Isaac’s head to bless him, and Isaac bent down to receive the blessing. And Abraham’s face was fatherliness itself, his look gentle, his speech full of exhortation. But Isaac could not understand him; his soul could not be lifted up. He threw his arms around Abraham’s knees, he fell pleading at his feet, he begged for his young life, for his bright hopes; he reminded him of the joy in Abraham’s house, he reminded him of the sorrow and the loneliness. Then Abraham raised the boy up and led him along by the hand, speaking words of comfort and exhortation. But Isaac could not understand him. Abraham climbed Mount Moriah, but Isaac did not understand him. Then Abraham turned away from him for a moment; but when Isaac looked at Abraham’s face a second time, it had changed. His look was wild, his figure was horror. He gripped Isaac by the chest, flung him to the ground and said: “Stupid boy, do you believe I am your father? I am an idol-worshipper. Do you believe it is God’s command? No, it is my own desire.” Then Isaac trembled and in his anxiety cried out: “God in heaven, have mercy on me! God of Abraham, have mercy on me! If I have no father on earth, be my father yourself!” But Abraham whispered to himself: “Lord in heaven, I thank you. After all, it is better that he believes I am a monster than that he loses his faith in you.”

When it is time to wean the child, the mother blackens her breast; it would surely be a shame for the breast to look so inviting when the child must not have it. Then the child believes the breast has changed; but the mother, she is the same, and her look is as loving and tender as ever. Happy the one who needed no more terrible means to wean the child!

It was early morning. Abraham rose early and embraced Sarah, the bride of his old age, and she kissed Isaac, her pride, her hope through all generations, who had taken away her shame. Then they rode in silence along the road, and Abraham’s eyes were fixed on the ground until the fourth day, when he raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah a long way off, but his eyes turned again to the ground. Without a word he arranged the wood and bound Isaac; without a word he drew the knife. Then he caught sight of the ram that God had chosen. That he sacrificed, and went home. — — — From that day on, Abraham aged; he could not forget that God had demanded it of him. Isaac flourished as before; but Abraham’s eye was darkened, and he saw joy no more.

When the child has grown big and it is time to wean it, the mother hides her bosom with a maiden’s modesty, and so the child no longer has a mother. Happy the child who did not lose its mother in any other way!

It was early morning. Abraham rose early and kissed Sarah, the young mother, and she kissed Isaac, her delight, her joy for all time. And Abraham rode along the road, lost in thought; he was thinking of Hagar and the son, whom he had driven out into the desert. He climbed Mount Moriah; he drew the knife.

It was a still evening. Abraham rode out alone, and he rode to Mount Moriah; he fell on his face and begged God to forgive him his sin — that he had wanted to sacrifice Isaac, that the father had forgotten his duty to the son. Many more times he rode that lonely road, but he could find no rest. To him it was incomprehensible that it should be a sin to have wanted to sacrifice to God the best thing he owned — the thing for which he would gladly have given his own life many times over. And supposing it was a sin — supposing he had not loved Isaac like that — then he could not understand that it could be forgiven; for what sin was more terrible?

When it is time to wean the child, the mother is not without sorrow either: sorrow that she and the child are separated more and more, that the child who first lay beneath her heart, and afterwards still rested at her breast, is no longer to be so near. So together they grieve the brief grief. Happy the one who kept the child so near, and did not need to grieve any more!

It was early morning. In Abraham’s house everything had been made ready for the journey. He took his leave of Sarah; the faithful servant Eliezer went with him a stretch of the way and then turned back. Abraham and Isaac rode on together in harmony until they reached Mount Moriah. But Abraham prepared everything for the sacrifice, calm and gentle; but as he turned away and drew the knife, Isaac saw Abraham’s left hand clench in despair and a trembling pass through his body — but Abraham drew the knife.

Then they came home again. Sarah hurried out to meet them, but Isaac had lost his faith. Nothing has ever been said of it in the world; Isaac never spoke to a living soul about what he had seen, and Abraham had no inkling that anyone had seen it.
When it is time to wean the child, the mother has the stronger food ready, so that the child shall not perish. Happy the one who has the stronger food ready.

In this way, and in many similar ways, the man of whom we are speaking thought about this event. And every time he came home after a journey to Mount Moriah, he sank down with weariness, folded his hands and said: “Still, there was no one as great as Abraham; who is capable of understanding him?”

chapters.title: Eulogy on Abraham
paragraphs: Suppose there were no eternal consciousness in a human being; suppose that underneath everything there were nothing but a wild, fermenting power which, twisting in obscure passions, produced all things, the great and the trivial alike; suppose that a bottomless void, never sated, lay concealed beneath everything — then what would life be, if not despair? Suppose it were so: suppose no holy bond held humanity together; suppose one generation sprang up after another like leaves in a wood; suppose one generation replaced another like birdsong in a wood; suppose our kind went through the world the way a ship goes through the sea, the way wind goes through the desert — a thoughtless, barren business; suppose an everlasting forgetfulness lay in wait, forever hungry, for its prey, and no power were strong enough to tear the prey from it — how empty life would be then, and how bleak! But that is exactly why it is not so. As God created man and woman, in the same way he shaped the hero and the poet — or the orator. Of what the hero does, the poet can do nothing; all he can do is admire the hero, love him, take delight in him. And yet he too is happy — no less happy than the hero. For the hero is, as it were, his better being, with which he is in love — glad that it is not himself after all, glad that his love can be admiration. He is the presiding spirit of recollection. All he can do is call to mind what has been done; all he can do is admire what has been done. He takes nothing from what is his own; he is jealous, rather, of what was entrusted to him. He follows the choice of his heart; but when he has found what he was looking for, he goes round to every man’s door with his song and his speech, so that everyone may admire the hero as he does and take pride in the hero as he does. That is his feat, his humble task; that is his loyal service in the house of the hero. If in this way he keeps faith with his love, struggling night and day with the craft of forgetfulness, which wants to spirit the hero away from him, then his task is complete, and he is united with the hero, who has loved him with the same fidelity. For the poet is, as it were, the hero’s better being: without force, admittedly, as a memory is, but transfigured too, as a memory is. So no one who was great shall be forgotten. Even if it takes a long while, even if a cloud of misunderstanding should carry the hero off, his lover will come all the same; and the longer time went on, the more faithfully he clings to him.

No! Not one who was great in the world shall be forgotten. But each was great in his own way, each in proportion to the greatness of what he loved. For the one who loved himself grew great by himself, and the one who loved others grew great by his devotion; but the one who loved God grew greater than everyone. Everyone shall be remembered, but each grew great in proportion to his expectation. One grew great by expecting the possible, another by expecting the eternal; but the one who expected the impossible grew greater than everyone. Everyone shall be remembered, but each was great in proportion to the magnitude of what he struggled with. For the one who struggled with the world grew great by conquering the world, and the one who struggled with himself grew greater by conquering himself; but the one who struggled with God grew greater than everyone. So there was struggle in the world, man against man, one against a thousand; but the one who struggled with God was greater than everyone. So there was struggle on earth: there was the one who conquered everything by his power, and there was the one who conquered God by his powerlessness. There was the one who relied on himself and won everything; there was the one who, secure in his strength, sacrificed everything; but the one who believed God was greater than everyone. There was the one who was great by his power, and the one who was great by his wisdom, and the one who was great by his hope, and the one who was great by his love; but Abraham was greater than everyone — great by the power whose strength is powerlessness, great by the wisdom whose secret is foolishness, great by the hope whose form is madness, great by the love that is hatred of oneself.

It was by faith that Abraham left the land of his fathers and became an alien in the land of the promise. One thing he left behind and one thing he took along: behind him he left his earthly good sense, and faith he took along. Otherwise, presumably, he would not have set out, but would have thought: this is unreasonable, after all. It was by faith that he was an alien in the land of the promise. Nothing there reminded him of what he held dear; instead everything, being new, tempted his soul toward a melancholy longing. And yet he was the one God had chosen, the one in whom the Lord took pleasure! Indeed, if he had been cast off, shut out from God’s grace, he could more easily have comprehended it; as it was, it looked like a mockery of him and of his faith. There was also one in the world who lived banished from the land of his fathers, which he loved. He has not been forgotten, and neither have his laments, when in his melancholy he searched for and found what he had lost. There is no lament from Abraham. Lamenting is human, weeping with the one who weeps is human; but having faith is greater, and contemplating the believer more blessed.

It was by faith that Abraham received the promise that every family on earth would be blessed in his seed. Time went on; the possibility was there; Abraham had faith. Time went on; it became unreasonable; Abraham had faith. There was one in the world who also had an expectation. Time went on, evening came near, and he was not so wretched as to forget his expectation, and for that reason he too shall not be forgotten. Then he sorrowed, and sorrow did not deceive him, as life had done. Sorrow did all it could for him, and in sorrow’s sweetness his disappointed expectation was his to keep. Sorrowing is human, sorrowing with the one who sorrows is human; but having faith is greater, and contemplating the believer more blessed. Of Abraham we have no song of sorrow. He did not count off the days in melancholy as the times went by; he did not eye Sarah suspiciously to see whether she was getting old; he did not stop the sun in its course to keep Sarah from aging, and his expectation with her; he did not lull Sarah with his melancholy song. Abraham grew old, and Sarah was mocked throughout the land; and yet he was the one God had chosen, the heir to the promise that every family on earth would be blessed in his seed. So it would surely have been better if God had not chosen him? What does it mean, being chosen by God? Does it mean that the wish of youth is refused you in youth, so that with great difficulty it may be fulfilled in old age? But Abraham had faith and held fast to the promise. If Abraham had wavered, he would have given it up, saying to God: “Perhaps, then, it is not your will after all that it should come to pass; in that case I will give up the wish. It was the only one I had; it was my blessedness. My soul is honest; I hide no secret grudge against you for refusing it.” He would not have been forgotten; many would have been saved by his example; but he would not have become the father of faith. For to give up one’s wish is great, but to hold it fast after one has given it up is greater; to grasp the eternal is great, but to hold fast to the temporal after one has given it up is greater. — Then the fullness of time came. If Abraham had not had faith, Sarah would probably have died of sorrow, and Abraham, blunted by grief, would not have understood the fulfillment and would have smiled at it the way one smiles at a dream from one’s youth. But Abraham had faith, and that is why he was young. For the one who always hopes for the best is deceived by life and grows old; the one who is always ready for the worst grows old early; but the one who has faith keeps an eternal youth. So praise be to that story! For Sarah, old as she was, was young enough to long for a mother’s joy, and Abraham, gray as he was, was young enough to wish to become a father. Outwardly, the wonder is that it happened as they had expected. In a deeper sense, faith’s wonder is this: Abraham and Sarah were young enough to wish, and faith had preserved their wish, and so their youth. He received the fulfillment of the promise; he received it in faith, and it came about according to the promise and according to faith. For Moses struck the rock with his rod, but he did not have faith.
Then there was gladness in Abraham’s house, when Sarah stood a bride on their golden wedding day.

But that was not how it was to stay; Abraham was to be put to the proof once more. He had fought against that crafty power which invents everything, against that watchful enemy who never slumbers, against that old man who outlives all things — he had fought against time and preserved his faith. Now the whole terror of the struggle was gathered into a single instant. “And God tempted Abraham and said to him: Take Isaac, your only son, whom you love; go to the land of Moriah, and there sacrifice him as a burnt offering on a mountain I will show you.”

So everything was wasted — more terrible than if it had never happened! So the Lord was merely making a mockery of Abraham! By a wonder he had made the unreasonable actual; now he wished to see it reduced to nothing again. It was foolishness, of course; but Abraham did not laugh at it, as Sarah laughed when the promise was announced. All was wasted! Seventy years of faithful expectation, the short-lived joy at faith’s fulfillment. Who is this, then, who tears the staff from the old man’s hand? Who is this who demands that the old man break it himself! Who is this who makes a man’s gray hairs inconsolable? Who is this who demands that he do it himself! Is there no pity for the venerable old man, none for the innocent child! And yet Abraham was the one God had chosen, and it was the Lord who laid the test on him. Now everything was to be wasted! The glorious remembrance of the generations, the promise in Abraham’s seed — only a whim, a passing thought the Lord had had, which Abraham must now blot out. That glorious treasure — as old as the faith in Abraham’s heart, older than Isaac by many, many years, the fruit of Abraham’s life, hallowed by prayers, ripened in battles — the blessing on Abraham’s lips: this was the fruit that must now be torn off untimely and made meaningless; for what meaning could it have, if Isaac was to be sacrificed! That melancholy yet blessed hour when Abraham was to say farewell to all that was dear to him, when he would once more lift his venerable head, when his countenance would shine like the Lord’s, when he would gather up his whole soul in a blessing strong enough to make Isaac blessed for all his days — that hour was never to come! For Abraham would indeed say farewell to Isaac, but it would be Abraham who remained behind; death would indeed part them, but it would be Isaac that death took as its prey. The old man would not, glad in death, lay his hand on Isaac in blessing; weary of life, he would lay a violent hand on Isaac. And it was God who was testing him. Yes, woe — woe to the messenger who had come to Abraham with news like this! Who would have dared to be the bearer of this sorrow? But it was God who was testing Abraham.

But Abraham had faith, and faith for this life. Indeed, had his faith concerned only a life to come, he would presumably have found it easier to throw everything away and hurry out of a world he did not belong to. But Abraham’s faith was not of that sort — if there is such a sort. For strictly speaking it is not faith, only faith’s remotest possibility, which dimly senses its object at the very edge of the horizon, yet is separated from it by a gaping chasm in which despair plays its game. But Abraham had faith precisely for this life: faith that he would live to old age in the land, held in honor among the people, blessed in his descendants, unforgettable in Isaac, the one dearest to him in life. He embraced Isaac with a love for which it was only a poor expression to say that he faithfully fulfilled a father’s duty to love his son — as indeed the summons itself also has it: “the son whom you love.” Jacob had twelve sons, and one he loved; Abraham had only one, whom he loved.

But Abraham had faith and did not doubt; he believed the unreasonable. Had Abraham doubted — then he would have done something different, something great and splendid; for how could Abraham have done anything that was not great and splendid! He would have made his way to Mount Moriah, chopped the firewood, set the pyre alight, drawn the knife; he would have called out to God: “Do not despise this sacrifice. It is not the best I own — that much I know; for what is an old man next to the child of the promise? But it is the best I am able to give you. Let Isaac never learn of it, so that he may find comfort in his youth.” He would have driven the knife into his own chest. The world would have admired him, and his name would never have been forgotten; yet being admired is one thing, and becoming a guiding star that saves the anxious is another.
But Abraham had faith. He did not pray for himself, hoping to move the Lord; only when the just punishment went forth over Sodom and Gomorrah did Abraham step forward with his prayers.

We read in those holy scriptures: “And God tempted Abraham and said: Abraham, Abraham, where are you? But Abraham replied: Here I am.” You to whom my words are addressed — was it like that with you? When you saw the heavy visitations coming toward you from afar, did you not tell the mountains, “Hide me,” and the hills, “Fall on me”? Or were you stronger? Even so, did your foot not drag slowly along the road — did it not seem to yearn back toward the old tracks? When the call came to you, did you answer, or did you not — perhaps quietly, in a whisper? Not so Abraham. Glad, bold, full of trust, he answered in a loud voice: Here I am. We read on: “And Abraham rose early in the morning.” He hastened as though to a feast, and early in the morning he was at the place appointed, on Mount Moriah. He said nothing to Sarah, nothing to Eliezer — and who, after all, could have understood him? Had the temptation not, by its very nature, exacted from him a vow of silence? “He chopped the firewood, he bound Isaac, he set the pyre alight, he drew the knife.” My listener! There were many fathers who believed that in their child they were losing the dearest thing they had in the world, and being robbed of all hope for the future; yet there was, after all, no one who was the child of the promise in the sense that Isaac was for Abraham. There were many fathers who lost their child; but then it was God — the Almighty’s unchanging and unsearchable will — whose hand took it. Not so with Abraham. A heavier test had been kept for him: along with the knife, Isaac’s fate had been laid in Abraham’s hand. There he stood, that old man, with his only hope! Yet he did not doubt; he cast no anxious glances right or left; he did not challenge heaven by his prayers. He knew it was God Almighty who was testing him; he knew that this was the heaviest sacrifice that could be demanded of him; but he knew too that no sacrifice was too heavy when God demanded it — and he drew the knife.

Who strengthened Abraham’s arm, who held his right hand raised so that it did not sink down powerless! Whoever looks at this is paralyzed. Who strengthened Abraham’s soul, so that his eyes did not go dark and he saw neither Isaac nor the ram! Whoever looks at this goes blind. — And yet rare enough, perhaps, is the one who is paralyzed and blinded; rarer still is the one who tells worthily what happened. We all know it — it was only a test.

If Abraham, standing on Mount Moriah, had doubted; if he had looked around him helplessly; if, before drawing the knife, he had happened to spot the ram; if God had allowed him to sacrifice it in Isaac’s place — then he would have traveled home, and everything would have been as it was: he would have Sarah, he would keep Isaac — and yet how altered it all would be! For his retreat would have been a flight, his rescue an accident, his reward disgrace, and his future, perhaps, perdition. Then he would have borne witness not to his faith, nor to God’s grace, but to how terrible a thing it is to go up Mount Moriah. Then Abraham would not have been forgotten, and nor would Mount Moriah. It would then be named not as Ararat is named, where the Ark came to rest, but named as a horror, because it was here that Abraham doubted.

Venerable Father Abraham! When you traveled home from Mount Moriah, you had no need of a eulogy to console you for what you had lost; for you had won everything and kept Isaac — was that not how it was? The Lord took him from you no more; you sat at table with him, joyful, in your tent, as you do in the beyond through all eternity. Venerable Father Abraham! Since those days thousands of years have run on, but you need no late-born lover to wrench your memory from the clutches of forgetfulness; for every language remembers you — and yet you reward your lover more gloriously than anyone does: in the beyond you make him blessed in your bosom, and here you captivate his eye and his heart with the marvel of your deed. Venerable Father Abraham! Second father of our kind! You, the first to perceive and bear witness to that immense passion which disdains the terrible battle with raging elements and the powers of creation, in order to struggle with God; you, the first to know that supreme passion, the holy, pure, humble expression of that divine madness which the pagans admired — forgive the one who set out to speak your praise, if he did not do it as he should. He spoke humbly, as his heart longed to; he spoke briefly, as is proper. But he will never forget that you needed a hundred years to receive a son in your old age against every expectation, and that you had to draw the knife before Isaac was yours to keep; he will never forget that for a hundred and thirty years you got no further than faith.

chapters.title: Preliminary Expectoration
paragraphs: An old saying, taken from the outward and visible world, says: “Only the one who works gets bread.” Strangely enough, the saying does not fit the world where it is most at home. For the outward world is subject to the law of imperfection, and there it happens again and again that the one who does not work also gets bread, and that the one who sleeps gets it more abundantly than the one who works. In the outward world everything belongs to whoever holds it. That world is in bondage to the law of indifference: the spirit of the ring obeys whoever has the ring, whether he is a Noureddin or an Aladdin, and whoever has the treasures of the world has them, however he came by them. In the world of spirit it is different. Here an eternal divine order reigns. Here it does not rain on the just and the unjust alike; here the sun does not shine on the good and the evil alike. Here it holds true that only the one who works gets bread; only whoever has been in anxiety finds rest; only whoever goes down into the underworld saves the beloved; only whoever draws the knife gets Isaac. The one who will not work does not get bread but is deceived, as the gods deceived Orpheus with an airy phantom in place of the beloved — deceived him because he was soft, not courageous; deceived him because he was a cithara player, not a man. Here it does no good to have Abraham for one’s father, or seventeen noble ancestors. What is written of the virgins of Israel fits the one who will not work: he brings forth wind. But whoever is willing to work brings forth his own father.

There is a kind of knowledge that presumptuously wants to bring into the world of spirit the same law of indifference under which the outward world groans. It thinks that it is enough to know what is great, and that no other work is needed. But for that very reason it does not get bread: it perishes of hunger while everything turns to gold. And what does it know, anyway? In the Greece of that time there were many thousands, and in later generations countless people, who knew all of Miltiades’ triumphs; but there was only one who was made sleepless by them. There have been countless generations who knew the story of Abraham by heart, word for word — how many has it made sleepless?

Now, the story of Abraham has the remarkable property that it always remains glorious, however poorly one understands it. Yet here again the question is whether one is willing to work and to be burdened. But people are not willing to work, and still they want to understand the story. They speak in Abraham’s honor — but how? They give the whole thing a perfectly commonplace expression: “What was great was that he loved God in such a way that he was willing to sacrifice the best to him.” That is very true; but “the best” is a vague expression. In the flow of thought and talk one quite confidently identifies Isaac with the best, and the one who meditates on it can smoke his pipe at his ease during the meditation, and the one who listens can stretch his legs out comfortably in front of him. If that rich young man whom Christ met on his way had sold all his goods and given them to the poor, we would praise him, as we praise everything great — though even him we would not understand without working. But he would still not have become an Abraham, even though he sacrificed the best. What is left out of Abraham’s story is the anxiety. For toward money I have no ethical obligation, but toward his son a father has the highest and holiest obligation of all. But anxiety is a dangerous business for the soft, and so it is forgotten; and nonetheless people want to talk about Abraham. Talk they do, and in the course of the talk the two expressions, Isaac and the best, are used interchangeably, and everything goes splendidly. Suppose, however, that among the listeners there happened to be a man who suffered from sleeplessness. Then the most terrible, the deepest misunderstanding, at once tragic and comic, lies very close at hand. He went home; he wanted to do just as Abraham did; for the son is, after all, the best. If that speaker got to hear of it, perhaps he went to the man, gathered all his clerical dignity and shouted: “You abominable man, you dregs of society, what devil has possessed you like this, that you would murder your son?” And the pastor, who had detected no warmth or sweat in himself when he preached about Abraham, was astonished at himself, at the earnest wrath with which he thundered down on that poor man. He was pleased with himself, for he had never spoken with such force and unction. He told himself and his wife: “I am an orator; all I lacked was the occasion. Last Sunday, when I spoke about Abraham, I was not moved in the least.” If this same speaker had some small surplus of understanding that he could afford to lose, I think he would lose it if the sinner answered calmly and with dignity: “But that is just what you yourself preached about last Sunday.” And how could the pastor ever have got such a thing into his head? Yet that is how it was, and the only mistake was that he had not known what he was saying. If only there were a poet who could make up his mind to prefer situations like this to the frippery and nonsense that comedies and novels are stuffed with! Here the comic and the tragic touch each other in absolute infinity. The pastor’s speech was perhaps ridiculous enough in and of itself, but it became infinitely ridiculous through its effect — and yet that effect was entirely natural. Or suppose the sinner, without raising any objection, really was converted by the pastor’s reprimand, and this zealous clergyman went home happy — happy in the awareness that he was effective not only from the pulpit but above all, with irresistible power, as a shepherd of souls: on Sunday he stirred the congregation to enthusiasm, while on Monday he stood like a cherub with a flaming sword before the man who by his deed wanted to put to shame that old saying that things in the world do not go as the pastor preaches.

If, on the other hand, the sinner was not convinced, his situation is tragic enough. He was then presumably executed or sent to the madhouse — in short, he became unhappy in relation to so-called actuality. In another sense, I rather think, Abraham made him happy; for the one who works does not perish.

How is one to explain a contradiction like that speaker’s? Is it because Abraham has acquired a prescriptive right to be a great man, so that whatever he does is great, while if someone else does the same it is sin, a sin that cries to heaven? In that case I do not wish to take part in such thoughtless praise. If faith cannot make it a holy act to be willing to murder one’s son, then let the verdict on Abraham be the same as on anyone else. If people perhaps lack the courage to carry their thought through, and to say that Abraham was a murderer, then surely it is better to acquire that courage than to waste time on undeserved eulogies. The ethical expression for what Abraham did is that he was willing to murder Isaac; the religious expression is that he was willing to sacrifice Isaac. But precisely in this contradiction lies the anxiety that can indeed make a person sleepless; and yet without this anxiety Abraham is not the one he is. Or perhaps Abraham did not do at all what the story tells; perhaps, because of the conditions of those times, it was something quite different. Then let us forget him; for what is the point of remembering a past that cannot become a present? Or perhaps that speaker had forgotten something that corresponds to the ethical forgetting of the fact that Isaac was the son. For when faith is taken away by being reduced to nil and nothing, all that remains is the raw fact that Abraham was willing to murder Isaac — and that is easy enough to imitate for anyone who does not have faith, that is, the faith that makes it hard for him.

I, for my part, am not short of courage to think a thought all the way through. Until now I have feared no thought. Should I ever come upon one, I hope I would at least have the honesty to say: This thought I fear; it sets something else in me in revolt, and therefore I will not think it. If I do wrong in this, the punishment will surely not fail to come. Had I recognized, as truth’s verdict, that Abraham was a murderer, I am not sure I could have silenced my reverence for him. But if I had thought it, I would presumably have kept silent about it; for one should not initiate others into thoughts like these. But Abraham is no illusion. He did not win his renown in his sleep, and he does not owe it to a whim of fate.

Can one, then, speak about Abraham without reserve, and not run the risk that someone will go astray and do the same? If I do not dare, I will keep entirely silent about Abraham; and above all I will not belittle him in such a way that he becomes, precisely through that, a snare for the weak. For if one makes faith everything — that is, what it is — then I think one dares to speak of it without danger in our time, which hardly runs to excess in faith; and it is only by faith that one comes to resemble Abraham, not by murder. If one makes love a fleeting mood, a sensual stirring in a person, then one only lays snares for the weak when one wants to talk about the exploits of love. Everyone, no doubt, has a passing movement of feeling; but if everyone therefore wanted to do the terrible thing that love has sanctified as an immortal exploit, then all is lost — both the exploit and the one who has gone astray.

So one could, I suppose, speak about Abraham; for what is great can never do harm when it is understood in its greatness. It is like a double-edged sword: it kills and it saves. If the lot fell to me to speak about it, I would start by showing how devout and God-fearing a man Abraham was, worthy to be called God’s elect. Only such a man is given such a test; but who is such a man? Next I would describe how Abraham loved Isaac. To that end I would ask all good spirits to stand by me, so that my speech might glow as a father’s love glows. I hope to portray it so that few fathers in all the King’s realms and lands would dare to claim that they loved like that. But if a father did not love as Abraham did, then surely any thought of sacrificing Isaac would be a spiritual trial — an inner assault on a person. One could already speak about this for several Sundays; there is no need to hurry, after all. The result, if it was spoken of rightly, would be that a good many fathers would not ask to hear any more at all, but for the time being would be glad if they really managed to love as Abraham loved. If there was then one who, after hearing what is great but also what is terrible in Abraham’s deed, dared to set out on the road, I would saddle my horse and ride with him. At every stage, until we came to Mount Moriah, I would explain to him that he could still turn back: he could repent of the misunderstanding that he was called to be put to the proof in such a struggle, and could confess that he lacked courage, so that God himself must take Isaac, if he would have him. I am convinced that such a person is not rejected, that he can attain blessedness along with everyone else — but not in time. Would people not, even in the most believing ages, judge such a person in this way? I have known a person who once could have saved my life, if he had been magnanimous. He put it plainly: “I can see well enough what I could do; but I do not dare. I fear that later I will lack the strength, that I will come to regret it.” He was not magnanimous; yet who would stop loving him on that account?

When I had spoken in this way, and had moved my listeners so that they had at least sensed the dialectical struggles of faith and its gigantic passion, I would not want to be to blame for an error on their part — that they should think: “He has faith to such a high degree; for us it is enough to hold on to his coat-tails.” For I would add: “I by no means have faith. I am by nature a shrewd head, and every such head always has great difficulty in making the movement of faith — though in and of itself I do not want to attach any value to that difficulty, as if overcoming it brought the shrewd head any further than the point that the simplest and most simple-hearted person reaches more easily.”

Love, after all, has its priests in the poets, and now and then one hears a voice that knows how to keep it in honor. But of faith one hears not a word. Who speaks to honor this passion? Philosophy goes further. Theology sits painted at the window, courting philosophy’s favor and offering her own beauty for sale to philosophy. Understanding Hegel is said to be hard; but understanding Abraham, that is a trifle. Going beyond Hegel is a marvel; but getting beyond Abraham, that is the easiest thing in the world. For my part, I have spent a good deal of time trying to understand the Hegelian philosophy, and I believe I have understood it reasonably well. I am rash enough to think that when, in spite of all my efforts, I cannot understand him in certain places, it is probably because he himself was not entirely clear. All this I do lightly and naturally; it does my head no harm. But when I have to think about Abraham, I am as if annihilated. At every moment I catch sight of that monstrous paradox that is the content of Abraham’s life; at every moment I am thrust back, and for all its passion my thought cannot penetrate it, cannot get a hair’s breadth further. I strain every muscle to get a view of it — and in the same instant I am paralyzed.

I am not unacquainted with what has been admired in the world as great and magnanimous. My soul feels its kinship with it and is assured, in all humility, that the cause the hero fought for was mine too. In the moment of contemplation I call out to myself: jam tua res agitur — now it is your own affair that is at stake. I can think myself into the hero; into Abraham I cannot think myself. When I have reached the summit, I fall, because what is offered me there is a paradox. Yet I by no means think that faith is something inferior on that account. On the contrary, I think it is the highest; and I think it is dishonest of philosophy to give out something else instead and to scoff at faith. Philosophy cannot give faith and is not supposed to; but it ought to understand itself, know what it is offering, and take nothing away — least of all cheat people out of something as though it were nothing. I am not unacquainted with the distress and dangers of life; I do not fear them, and I go to meet them boldly. I am no stranger to the terrible. My memory is a faithful wife, and my imagination is — what I myself am not — an industrious little girl who sits quietly at her work all day and in the evening knows how to chatter to me so prettily that I cannot help looking at it, although what she paints is not always landscapes or flowers or Schäfer-Historier (shepherds’ idylls). I have looked the terrible in the eye; I do not flee from it in fear. But I know very well that even if I go to meet it with courage, my courage is still not the courage of faith, and is nothing to be compared with it. I cannot make the movement of faith. I cannot shut my eyes and plunge trustingly into the absurd; for me it is an impossibility — but I do not pride myself on that. I am convinced that God is love; this thought has for me a primal lyrical validity. When the thought is present to me, I am unspeakably blessed; when it is absent, I long for it more fiercely than a lover longs for the one he loves. But I do not have faith; this is the courage I lack. God’s love is, for me, in both a direct and an inverse sense, incommensurable — not measurable by any common standard — with the whole of actuality. I am not cowardly enough to whimper and complain about that, but neither am I underhanded enough to deny that faith is something far higher. I can bear living in my own way well enough; I am glad and content. But my joy is not faith’s joy, and compared with that it is unhappy. I do not bother God with my small sorrows; particular things do not concern me; I keep my eyes on my love alone and keep its virginal flame clean and clear. Faith is convinced that God concerns himself with the smallest things. I am content in this life to be married with the left hand; faith is humble enough to demand the right. For that this is humility I do not deny, and never shall.

Is everyone in my time really capable of making the movements of faith? Unless I am much mistaken about my time, it tends rather to pride itself on doing what it presumably does not even think me capable of — namely, the imperfect. It goes against my soul to do what is so often done: to speak inhumanly about what is great, as if a few thousand years were an immense distance. I prefer to speak of it humanly, as if it had happened yesterday, and to let only greatness itself be the distance, a distance that either lifts up or judges. If, then (in the capacity of a tragic hero, for higher I cannot come), I had been summoned to such an extraordinary journey in the king’s service as the one to Mount Moriah, I know perfectly well what I would have done. I would not have been such a coward as to stay at home; I would not have dawdled along the highway either, or forgotten the knife to cause a little delay. I am fairly sure that I would have been there on the stroke of the hour, with everything in order — perhaps I would, if anything, have come too early, so that it could be over soon. But I also know what else I would have done. The moment I got up on the horse, I would have told myself: Now everything is lost. God demands Isaac; I sacrifice him, and all my joy with him — and yet God is love, and remains love for me. For in temporality God and I cannot talk with each other; we share no language. Perhaps someone or other in our time will be foolish enough, and envious enough of what is great, to want to persuade himself and me that had I really done this, I would have done something still greater than Abraham; for my enormous resignation was far more ideal and poetic than Abraham’s pettiness. And yet this is the greatest untruth; for my enormous resignation was the substitute for faith. Nor, then, could I do more than make the infinite movement, so as to find myself and to rest in myself again. Nor would I have loved Isaac as Abraham loved him. That I was resolute enough to make the movement might prove my courage, humanly speaking. That I loved him with all my soul is the premise without which the whole thing becomes a misdeed. But still I would not have loved as Abraham did; for then I would have held back even at the very last minute — without thereby arriving at Mount Moriah too late. Moreover, by my conduct I would have ruined the whole story; for had I received Isaac back, I would have been at a loss. What came easiest to Abraham would have been hard for me: to be glad in Isaac again! For the one who, with the whole infinity of his soul, proprio motu et propriis auspiciis — of his own motion and on his own authority — has made the infinite movement and can do no more, keeps Isaac only in pain.

But what did Abraham do? He came neither too early nor too late. He mounted the donkey and rode slowly along the road. All that time he had faith: he believed that God would not require Isaac of him, while he was nevertheless willing to sacrifice him when it was demanded. He believed by virtue of the absurd; for human calculation was out of the question, and surely it was the absurd that God, who was requiring this of him, would take the requirement back the very next moment. He climbed the mountain, and even at the moment when the knife flashed, he believed — that God would not require Isaac. So he was no doubt surprised by the outcome; but through a double movement he had arrived at his first condition, and so he received Isaac more gladly than the first time. Let us go further. Let us suppose that Isaac really is sacrificed. Abraham had faith. He did not believe that he would one day be blessed in the world beyond, but that he would be blessed with happiness here in this world. God could give him a new Isaac, could call the sacrificed one back to life. He believed by virtue of the absurd; for all human calculation had long since come to an end. That grief can drive a person out of his mind — that one sees, and it is hard enough. That there is a strength of will that can sail so close to the wind that it saves the understanding, even if the person becomes a little strange — that one also sees, and I do not mean to belittle it. But to be able to lose one’s understanding, and with it the whole of finitude, for which the understanding is the exchange broker, and then by virtue of the absurd to win back exactly the same finitude — that appalls my soul. Yet I do not say for that reason that it is something lowly; on the contrary, it is the only marvel. People generally suppose that faith turns out no work of art — that what it produces is rough, crude work, fit only for the clumsier natures. But the truth is quite otherwise. Of all things, the dialectic of faith is the most delicate and the most remarkable. It has an elevation I can certainly picture to myself, but no more. I can make the great springboard leap by which I pass over into infinity. I have a back like a rope-dancer’s, twisted when I was a child, so this comes easily to me: one, two, three, and I can walk on my head in existence. The next step, though, I cannot take; for the marvelous I cannot do — I can only stand amazed at it. Indeed, if Abraham, at the moment he swung his leg over the donkey’s back, had told himself, “Isaac is lost now; I could just as well sacrifice him here at home as travel all that long way to Moriah” — then I have no need of Abraham. As it is, I bow seven times to his name and seventy times to his deed. For he did no such thing, as I can prove from the fact that he was glad to receive Isaac, heartily glad, and that he needed no preparation, no time to collect himself for finitude and its joy. If that had not been how things stood with Abraham, then perhaps he would have loved God, but he would not have had faith. For the one who loves God without faith reflects on himself; the one who loves God in faith reflects on God.

Abraham stands at this summit. The last stage he loses sight of is infinite resignation — the movement by which one gives up the finite and finds one’s peace in the eternal. He really does go further, and comes to faith. For all these caricatures of faith — the miserable, lukewarm sloth that thinks, “There’s surely nothing to worry about; it isn’t worth grieving before the time comes,” the paltry hope that says, “One can’t know what will happen; it might just be possible” — these caricatures belong to the wretchedness of life, and infinite resignation has already infinitely despised them.

I cannot understand Abraham; in a certain sense, I can learn nothing from him except to be astonished. If people imagine that by considering the outcome of that story they might let themselves be moved to have faith, they deceive themselves and want to cheat God of the first movement of faith; they want to suck wisdom for living out of the paradox. Perhaps one or two may succeed at it; for our age does not stop at faith, nor at faith’s miracle of making water into wine; it goes further and makes wine into water.

Would it not be best, though, to stop at faith, and is it not outrageous that everyone wants to go further? When people in our time — and this is proclaimed in various ways — will not stop at love, where do they end up? In earthly shrewdness and petty calculation, in paltriness and wretchedness, in everything that can make a human being’s divine origin doubtful. Would it not be best to stop at faith, and for the one who stands to take care that he does not fall? For the movement of faith must constantly be made by virtue of the absurd — but, note carefully, in such a way that one does not lose finitude but gains it whole and entire. As for me, I can indeed describe the movements of faith, but I cannot make them. If you want to learn the movements of swimming, you can have yourself hung in a harness from the ceiling; you may well describe the movements, but you do not swim. Just so, I can describe the movements of faith; but when I am tossed into the water, I do swim, admittedly (for I am not one of the waders), yet my movements are different. They are the movements of infinity, while faith does the reverse: having made the movements of infinity, it makes those of finitude. Happy is the one who can make these movements! He does the marvelous, and I shall never tire of admiring him. Whether it is Abraham or the slave in Abraham’s household, a professor of philosophy or some poor maidservant, is absolutely indifferent to me; I look only at the movements. But at those I do look, and I let no one take me in — neither myself nor anyone else. The knights of infinite resignation are easy to recognize: their gait is gliding, bold. Those, on the other hand, who carry the jewel of faith are apt to deceive, because their outward appearance bears a striking resemblance to what both infinite resignation and faith deeply despise: philistinism, the outlook of the philistine — the narrow, comfortable townsman.

I frankly confess that in my practice I have not come across a single reliable specimen — though I do not therefore mean to deny that perhaps every other person is such a specimen. All the same, I have been tracking one down for several years, in vain. People generally travel round the world to see rivers and mountains, new stars, gaudy birds, misshapen fish, ridiculous races of mankind; they give themselves over to the animal stupor that gawks at existence, and believe they have seen something. None of that engages me. If, however, I knew where such a knight of faith lived, I would make the journey to him on foot; for this marvel engages me absolutely. I would not let him out of my sight for an instant; every minute I would watch how he went about the movements. I would consider myself provided for in life, and divide my time between watching him and doing the exercises myself, and so spend all my time admiring him. As I said, I have not found anyone of the kind; but I can certainly conceive of him. Here he is. The introduction takes place; I am presented to him. The moment I first set eyes on him, in that same instant I thrust him away from me, make a leap backward myself, clap my hands together and say half aloud, “Good Lord! Is this the man? Is it really him? Why, he looks like a tax collector!” But it is him all the same. I draw a little closer to him and watch his slightest movement, to see whether some small, incongruous fragment of a signal might not show itself from the infinite — a glance, a look, a gesture, a touch of melancholy, a smile — that betrayed the infinite in its incongruity with the finite. No! I examine his figure from head to toe, to see whether there might not be a crack through which the infinite peeped out. No! He is solid through and through. His footing? It is sturdy, and belongs wholly to finitude; no dressed-up citizen walking out to Frederiksberg on a Sunday afternoon treads the ground more firmly. He belongs wholly to the world; no philistine could belong to it more. Nothing is to be detected of that strange and superior air by which one recognizes the knight of infinity. He takes delight in everything and takes part in everything; and every time one sees him take part in something in particular, he does it with a persistence that marks the earthly man whose soul is bound up with such things. He attends to his work. Seeing him at it, one would think he was a clerk who had lost his soul in Italian double-entry bookkeeping, so punctual is he. He takes Sundays off. He goes to church. No heavenly gaze, no sign of the incommensurable gives him away; without knowing him, one could not possibly single him out from the rest of the crowd, for his hearty, vigorous hymn-singing proves at most that he has a good pair of lungs. In the afternoon he walks out to the woods. He delights in everything he sees: in the bustle of people, the new omnibuses, the Sound. When one meets him on the Strandvej, one would think he was a petty shopkeeper out on the town for once — that is exactly how he enjoys himself; for he is no poet, and I have tried in vain to worm out of him the incommensurability of the poet. Toward evening he walks home, his gait as tireless as a postman’s. On the way he thinks that his wife is sure to have a special little hot dish waiting for him when he gets home — a roast lamb’s head with vegetables, for example. If he met a kindred spirit, he could go on all the way to Østerport talking with him about this dish, with a passion worthy of a restaurant keeper. As it happens, he does not have four skilling to his name, and yet he believes firmly and fully that his wife has that delicious dish waiting for him. If she has it, it would be an enviable sight for people of rank, and an inspiring one for ordinary folk, to watch him eat; for his appetite outdoes Esau’s. His wife has no such dish — and, oddly enough, he is exactly the same. Along the way he goes past a building lot and runs into another man. They chat for a moment; in a flash he raises a building, and he has every resource at his command to do it. The stranger leaves him thinking that this must surely be a capitalist, while my admired knight thinks, “Yes, if it came to that, I could easily get it.” He leans out of an open window and looks at the square where he lives, at everything that goes on there — a rat slipping in under the plank over the gutter, the children playing. Everything engages him, with a calm in existence as if he were a girl of sixteen. And yet he is no genius; for I have tried in vain to spy out the incommensurability of genius in him. Of an evening he smokes his pipe; to look at him, you would swear it was the grocer from across the street, vegetating in the twilight. He lets things take their course with an unconcern as if he were a feckless good-for-nothing; and yet at every moment he lives he buys up the opportune time at the dearest price, for he does not do even the smallest thing except by virtue of the absurd. And yet, and yet — indeed, I could become furious about it, if only out of envy — and yet this man has made the movement of infinity, and makes it at every moment. In infinite resignation he drains the deep melancholy of existence; the blessedness of infinity is known to him; he has experienced the pain of forsaking everything, whatever is dearest to one in the world. And yet finitude tastes every bit as good to him as to someone who never knew anything higher; for his staying in finitude bore no trace of a cowed and anxious drilling, and yet he has the confidence to delight in it as if it were the most certain thing of all. And yet, and yet, the whole earthly shape he brings forth is a new creation by virtue of the absurd. He resigned everything infinitely, and then he took hold of everything again by virtue of the absurd. He constantly makes the movement of infinity, but he makes it with such precision and assurance that he constantly gets finitude out of it, and there is not a second in which one suspects anything else. It is said to be the hardest task for a dancer to leap into a particular position in such a way that there is not a single second in which he is reaching for the position, but in the leap itself he stands in the position. Perhaps no dancer can do it — but that knight does. Most people live lost in worldly sorrow and joy; they are the ones who sit out and do not get into the dance. The knights of infinity are dancers and have elevation. They make the movement upward and come down again; and this too is a pastime not without its blessedness, and not unlovely to watch. But every time they come down, they cannot take up the position at once; they waver for a moment, and this wavering shows that they are strangers in the world after all. It is more or less conspicuous according to how much art they have; but not even the most artful of these knights can conceal the wavering. One need not see them in the air; one need only see them at the moment they touch the ground and have touched it — and one knows them. But to be able to come down in such a way that in the same second one looks as if one were standing and walking; to turn the leap in life into walking; to express the sublime absolutely in the pedestrian — that is what only that knight can do, and it is the only marvel.

But this marvel can so easily deceive, so I will describe the movements in a particular case that can shed light on their relation to actuality; for that is what everything turns on. A young man falls in love with a princess, and the whole content of his life lies in this love; and yet the circumstances are such that it is impossible for this love to be realized, impossible for it to be translated out of ideality into reality. The slaves of wretchedness, the frogs in life’s swamp, naturally shriek: “Such a love is folly; the rich brewer’s widow is every bit as good and solid a match.” Let them croak undisturbed in the swamp. That is not what the knight of infinite resignation does; he does not give up his love, not for all the splendor in the world. He is no simpleton. He first assures himself that it truly is his life’s content, and his soul is too sound and too proud to squander the least thing on an infatuation. He is not cowardly; he is not afraid to let the love steal into his most secret, his most remote thoughts, to let it wind itself in countless coils around every ligament of his consciousness — if the love becomes unhappy, he will never be able to tear himself free of it. He feels a blessed rapture in letting the love thrill through every nerve of his; and yet his soul is as solemn as that of someone who has drained the cup of poison and feels the juice seep through every drop of his blood — for this moment is life and death. When he has thus drawn the whole love into himself and immersed himself in it, he has courage enough to try everything and risk everything. He surveys the circumstances of his life; he summons the swift thoughts, which like well-trained doves obey his every signal; he swings his staff over them, and they scatter every way. But when they now all come back, all of them as messengers of sorrow, and explain to him that it is an impossibility, he grows quiet. He dismisses them, he is left alone, and then he undertakes the movement. If what I am saying here is to have any meaning, then everything depends on the movement taking place in the proper way. In the first place, then, the knight will have the strength to concentrate the whole content of life and the meaning of actuality in one single wish. If a person lacks this concentration, this self-containment — if his soul is scattered from the start among the many things — then he will never get as far as making the movement. He will act prudently in life, like the financiers who put their capital into all sorts of securities in order to gain on the one when they lose on the other: in short, he is no knight. In the second place, the knight will have the strength to concentrate the whole result of his operations of thought in one act of consciousness. If he lacks this self-containment, if his soul is scattered from the start among the many things, he will never find the time to make the movement. He will forever be running errands in life, never going into eternity; for even at the moment he is nearest to it, he will suddenly discover that he has forgotten something he has to go back for. In the next moment, he will think, it will be possible — and that is quite true, too. But by such considerations one never gets as far as making the movement; with their help one only sinks deeper and deeper into the mire.

So the knight makes the movement — but which movement? Will he forget the whole thing — for there is a kind of concentration in that too, is there not? No! For the knight does not contradict himself, and it is a contradiction to forget all that one’s life contained and still remain the same. He has no urge to become someone else, and he by no means considers that the great thing. Only the lower natures forget themselves and become something new. The butterfly, for instance, has entirely forgotten that it was a caterpillar; perhaps it can in turn forget so entirely that it was a butterfly that it can become a fish. The deeper natures never forget themselves; they never turn into anything but what they were. So the knight will remember everything; but this remembering is precisely the pain, and yet in infinite resignation he is reconciled with existence. For him, his love for that princess became the expression of an eternal love. It took on a religious character; it was transfigured into a love for the eternal being — who did, it is true, deny the fulfillment, but who nevertheless reconciled him again in the eternal consciousness that his love is valid in a form of eternity that no actuality can take from him. Fools and young people prattle that for a human being everything is possible. But this is a grave error. In terms of spirit, all things are possible; but in the world of finitude a great deal is not. Yet the knight makes this impossibility possible by expressing it spiritually — and he expresses it spiritually by renouncing it. The wish that would have led him out into actuality, but was wrecked on the impossibility, is now bent inward; yet that does not mean it is lost, nor is it forgotten. Sometimes it is the dim stirrings of the wish within him that awaken the memory; sometimes he awakens it himself. For he is too proud to want what was the whole content of his life to have been the affair of a fleeting moment. He keeps this love young, and it grows with him in years and in beauty. Yet he needs no finite occasion to make it grow. From the moment he has made the movement, the princess is lost. He has no need of those erotic tremblings of the nerves at the sight of the beloved, and so on. Nor does he need, in the finite sense, to be forever taking leave of her, because in the eternal sense he remembers her. And he knows very well that lovers who are so keen to see each other once more, in farewell, for the last time, are right to be keen, and right to think that it is the last time; for they are the ones who forget each other soonest. He has understood the deep secret that even in loving another human being one ought to be sufficient to oneself. He no longer takes any finite account of what the princess does, and that is exactly the proof that he has made the movement infinitely. This is where one can get to see whether the movement in the single individual is true or feigned. Someone else, too, believed he had made the movement; but, look, time went on, and the princess did something else — married a prince, for instance — and then his soul lost the elasticity of resignation. By this he showed that he had not made the movement correctly; for whoever has resigned infinitely is sufficient to himself. The knight does not cancel his resignation. He preserves his love as young as it was in its first moment; he never lets it slip from him, precisely because he has made the movement infinitely. Nothing the princess does can disturb him. Only the lower natures find the law for their actions in another human being — the premises of their actions outside themselves. If, on the other hand, the princess is of a like mind, then something beautiful will come of it. She will then introduce herself into that order of knighthood into which no one is admitted by ballot, but of which everyone is a member who has the courage to introduce himself — the order of knighthood that proves its immortality by making no distinction between man and woman. She, too, will preserve her love young and healthy; she, too, will have got over her anguish, even if she does not, as the old song has it, “lie every night at her lord’s side.” These two will then suit each other for all eternity, with a harmonia praestabilita — a pre-established harmony — so perfectly in time that if ever the moment came (a moment that does not, however, occupy them in the finite sense, for then they would grow old), if ever the moment came that allowed their love to be given its expression in time, they would be able to begin exactly where they would have begun if they had been united from the start. Anyone who understands this, man or woman, can never be deceived; for only the lower natures imagine that they have been deceived. No girl who is not this proud really knows how to love; but if she is this proud, then all the cunning and cleverness in the world cannot deceive her.

In infinite resignation there is peace and rest. Every human being who wills it — who has not debased himself by holding himself in contempt, which is even more terrible than being too proud — can train himself to make this movement, which, in its pain, reconciles a person to existence. Infinite resignation is that shirt spoken of in an old folk tale. The thread is spun under tears, bleached with tears, the shirt sewn in tears; but then it also protects better than iron and steel. The imperfection in the folk tale is that a third party can make up this linen. The secret of life is that everyone has to sew it for himself; and the remarkable thing is that a man can sew it every bit as well as a woman. In infinite resignation there is peace and rest and consolation in pain — provided, that is, the movement is made normally. I could, however, easily write a whole book if I set out to go through the various misunderstandings, the back-to-front positions, the sloppy movements I have come across in my own small practice alone. People believe very little in spirit; and yet it is precisely spirit that matters in making this movement. What matters is that the movement not be the one-sided result of a dira necessitas — a harsh necessity — and the more that necessity is present, the more doubtful it always becomes whether the movement is normal. So if one means to hold that cold, barren necessity must necessarily be present, one is saying that no one can experience death before he really dies — which strikes me as crass materialism. But in our time people care less about making pure movements. Suppose someone who was to learn dancing said: “Generation upon generation has now spent centuries learning the positions; it is high time I turned this to my advantage and started straight in on the française.” People would probably laugh at him a little; but in the world of spirit this is found extremely plausible. What, then, is cultivation? I thought it was the course the single individual runs through in order to catch up with himself; and whoever will not go through this course is helped very little by having been born in the most enlightened age.

Infinite resignation is the final stage preceding faith, so that whoever has not made this movement is without faith. For it is only in infinite resignation that I become clear to myself in my eternal validity, and not until then can there be talk of grasping existence by virtue of faith.

Let us now have the knight of faith appear in the case described. He does precisely what the other knight does. He gives up, infinitely, the love that is his life’s content, and he is reconciled in the pain. But then the marvel occurs: he makes yet another movement, more wondrous than anything, for he says: “I believe nevertheless that I will get her — by virtue, that is, of the absurd, by virtue of this: that for God everything is possible.” The absurd does not belong among the distinctions that lie within the understanding’s own range. It is not the same thing as the improbable, the unexpected, the unlooked-for. At the moment the knight resigned, he assured himself of the impossibility, humanly speaking; this was the understanding’s result, and he had energy enough to think it. In the infinite sense, on the other hand, it was possible — namely, by resigning it. But this possessing is, of course, at the same time a giving up; and yet for the understanding this possessing is no absurdity. For the understanding went on being right that in the world of wretchedness where it rules, it was and remained an impossibility. The knight of faith is just as clearly conscious of this. Accordingly, nothing can save him but the absurd, and this he grasps by faith. He acknowledges the impossibility, then, and in the same moment he believes the absurd. For if he wants to imagine that he has faith without acknowledging the impossibility with all the passion of his soul and with his whole heart, he deceives himself, and his testimony has no footing anywhere, since he has not even come as far as infinite resignation.

Faith is therefore not an aesthetic emotion (the aesthetic being the sphere of immediate feeling) but something far higher, precisely because resignation comes before it. It is not the immediate impulse of the heart, but the paradox of existence. So when a young girl, in spite of all difficulties, nevertheless remains certain that her wish will indeed be fulfilled, this certainty is not at all the certainty of faith — even though she has been brought up by Christian parents and has perhaps gone to the pastor for instruction for a whole year. She is certain in all her childlike naivety and innocence.
