This certainty, too, ennobles her being and gives her a supernatural stature, so that like a thaumaturge — a worker of wonders — she can conjure the finite powers of existence and bring even stones to weep; while, on the other hand, in her fluster she is as likely to run to Herod as to Pilate, touching all the world with her pleading. Her certainty is most lovable, and one can learn much from her; but there is one thing one does not learn from her: one does not learn to make movements. For her certainty does not dare to look the impossibility in the eye, in the pain of resignation.

I can understand, then, that making the infinite movement of resignation requires strength and energy and freedom of spirit; I can also understand that it is feasible. The next thing astonishes me; my brain turns over in my head. For after having made the movement of resignation, then by virtue of the absurd to get everything — to get the wish, whole and undiminished — that is beyond human powers; it is a marvel. But this I can understand: that the young girl’s certainty is mere light-mindedness compared with the unshakability of faith, even though faith’s unshakability has seen the impossibility. Every time I want to make this movement, everything goes black before my eyes; in the same moment I admire it absolutely, and in the same moment a tremendous anxiety seizes my soul — for what, then, is it to tempt God? And yet this movement is the movement of faith, and it goes on being so, even if philosophy, to confuse the concepts, would have us believe that it has faith, and even if theology wants to sell it off cheap.

No faith is needed in order to resign. For what I win in resignation is my eternal consciousness; that is a purely philosophical movement, one I am confident I can make when it is demanded, and one I can discipline myself to make. For every time some bit of finitude threatens to get the better of me, I starve myself out until I make the movement; for my eternal consciousness is my love of God, and that ranks higher for me than anything. No faith is needed in order to resign; but faith is needed in order to get the very least thing more than my eternal consciousness, for this is what is paradoxical. The movements are often confused. People say that one needs faith in order to renounce everything. Indeed, one hears something stranger still: a person complains that he has lost his faith, and when one checks the scale to see where he stands, one sees, strangely enough, that he has only reached the point at which he ought to make the infinite movement of resignation. In resignation I renounce everything. I make this movement on my own; and if I fail to make it, that is because I am cowardly and effete and lacking in enthusiasm, and have no feeling for the significance of the lofty dignity allotted to every human being: that of being his own censor — a far more distinguished office than being censor general of the entire Roman Republic. I make this movement on my own, and what I thereby win is myself in my eternal consciousness, in blessed understanding with my love for the eternal being. By faith I renounce nothing; on the contrary, by faith I get everything — precisely in the sense in which it is said that whoever has faith as a grain of mustard seed can move mountains. A purely human courage is needed to renounce all of temporality in order to win eternity. But eternity I do win, and I can never in all eternity renounce it; that would be a self-contradiction. But a paradoxical and humble courage is needed to grasp, after that, the whole of temporality by virtue of the absurd — and this courage is faith’s. By faith Abraham did not give Isaac up; by faith Abraham got Isaac. By virtue of resignation that rich young man ought to have given everything away; but when he had done so, the knight of faith should have said to him: “By virtue of the absurd you will get every last penny back, provided you can believe it.” And these words ought by no means to be a matter of indifference to the formerly rich young man; for if he gave his possessions away because he was sick of them, then his resignation was in a sorry state.

Temporality, finitude — that is what everything turns on. By my own powers I can resign everything, and then find peace and rest in pain. I can bear everything — even if that dreadful demon, more terrible than the skeleton Death who frightens people, even if madness held up the fool’s costume before my eyes and I understood from its look that it was I who was to put it on. I can still save my soul, as long as it matters more to me that my love for God should triumph in me than that I should have earthly happiness. Even in this last moment a person can gather his whole soul in one single glance toward the heaven from which every good gift comes; and this glance will be understood, by him and by the one it seeks, to mean that he stayed true to his love after all. Then he will calmly put on the costume. Anyone whose soul lacks this romance has sold his soul, whether he got a kingdom for it or a miserable piece of silver. But by my own powers I cannot get the least of what belongs to finitude; for I am constantly using my powers to resign everything. By my own powers I can give up the princess, and I will not turn into a sourpuss; I will find joy and peace and rest in my pain. But by my own powers I cannot get her back, for it is precisely to resign that I am using my powers. But by faith, says that wonderful knight — by faith you will get her, by virtue of the absurd.

This movement, you see, I cannot make. As soon as I want to begin on it, everything turns upside down, and I flee back into the pain of resignation. I can swim in life, but for this mystical hovering I am too heavy. To exist so that at every moment my opposition to existence expresses itself as the most beautiful and secure harmony with it — that I cannot do. And yet it must be glorious to get the princess. I say so at every moment, and the knight of resignation who does not say so is a fraud: he has not had a single wish, and he has not kept the wish young in his pain. Perhaps there was one who found it convenient enough that the wish was no longer alive, that the arrow of pain had been blunted; but someone like that is no knight. A free-born soul who caught himself at it would despise himself and start over, and above all would not let his soul be deceived by itself. And yet it must be glorious to get the princess. And yet only the knight of faith is happy — the hereditary lord of the finite — while the knight of resignation is a stranger and a foreigner. To get the princess in this way, to live happily and joyfully day in and day out with her (for this too was conceivable, of course: that the knight of resignation might get the princess — but his soul had seen through the impossibility of their future happiness); in this way to live happily and joyfully every moment by virtue of the absurd, at every moment to see the sword hovering above the head of the beloved, and yet to find not rest in the pain of resignation but joy by virtue of the absurd — that is wonderful. Whoever does it is great, the only great one. The thought of it moves my soul, which was never stingy in admiring what is great.

Suppose, now, that everyone of my own time who will not stop at faith really is a man who has comprehended the horror of life, who has understood what Daub means when he says that a soldier standing alone at his post with a loaded rifle, by a powder magazine, on a stormy night, gets strange thoughts. Suppose that everyone who will not stop at faith really is a man who had the strength of soul to comprehend the thought that the wish was an impossibility, and who then took time to be alone with that thought. Suppose that everyone who will not stop at faith is a man who was reconciled in pain and reconciled by pain. Suppose that everyone who will not stop at faith is a man who then (and if he has not done all of the foregoing, he need not trouble himself when faith is under discussion) did the wonderful thing and grasped the whole of existence by virtue of the absurd. Then what I am writing is the highest eulogy on my contemporaries, by the least among them — one who could make only the movement of resignation. But in that case why will people not stop at faith? Why does one sometimes hear that people are embarrassed to confess that they have faith? This I cannot comprehend. If I ever get so far as to be able to make this movement, then from that day on I shall drive a coach and four.

Is it really so? Is all the philistinism I see in life — which I let my deed, not my word, pass judgment on — really not what it seems? Is it the marvel? That is conceivable, after all; for that hero of faith did bear a striking resemblance to it — since that hero of faith was not even an ironist and humorist, but something still higher. There is a great deal of talk in our time about irony and humor, especially from people who have never managed to practice them, but who nonetheless know how to explain everything. I am not wholly a stranger to these two passions; I know somewhat more about them than is to be found in German and German-Danish compendiums. So I know that these two passions differ essentially from the passion of faith. Irony and humor also reflect on themselves, and therefore belong in the sphere of infinite resignation; they have their elasticity in the fact that the individual is incommensurable with actuality.

The last movement, the paradoxical movement of faith, I cannot make — be it a duty or whatever it may be — although I would be only too glad to. Whether a person has the right to say this must be left to him; it becomes a matter between him and the eternal being who is the object of faith, whether he can come to an amicable settlement on this point. What every human being can do is make the movement of infinite resignation; and I for my part would not hesitate to call anyone a coward who wants to imagine that he cannot. With faith it is another matter. But what no human being has the right to do is to talk others into imagining that faith is a small thing, or an easy matter, when it is the greatest and the hardest thing of all.

People take the story of Abraham another way. They praise God’s grace for granting him Isaac again — the whole thing was only a test. A test — this word can say a lot or a little, and yet the whole business is over the moment it is said. One climbs onto a winged horse; in the same instant one is on Mount Moriah; in the same instant one sees the ram. One forgets that Abraham rode only on a donkey, which goes slowly along the road; that he had a three-day journey; that he needed some time to split the firewood, to bind Isaac and to sharpen the knife.

And yet people praise Abraham. The one who is to speak can quite well sleep until the last quarter of an hour before he has to speak; the listener can quite well fall asleep during the speech; for everything goes easily enough, without trouble on either side. If there were a man present who suffered from sleeplessness, then perhaps he went home, sat down in a corner and thought: “The whole thing is a matter of a moment. Just wait a minute and you will see the ram, and the test is over.” If the speaker came upon him in this state, I imagine he would plant himself before him in all his dignity and say: “You wretch, that you can let your soul sink into such foolishness! No miracle happens, and the whole of life is a test.” As the speaker went on with his outpouring, he got more and more worked up and grew more and more pleased with himself; and whereas he had noticed no rush of blood to the head while he was speaking about Abraham, he now felt the vein swelling in his forehead. Perhaps he would be struck dumb if the sinner answered calmly and with dignity: “But that is what you preached about last Sunday.”

So let us either strike Abraham out altogether, or let us learn to be horrified at the tremendous paradox that is the meaning of his life, so that we may understand that our time, like every time, can be glad if it has faith. If Abraham is not a nullity, a phantom, a bauble one plays with to pass the time, then the error can never lie in the sinner’s wanting to do the same. What matters is to see how great a thing it was that Abraham did, so that the man can judge for himself whether he has the calling and the courage to be put to the proof in such a thing. The comic contradiction in the speaker’s conduct was that he made Abraham into something insignificant, and yet wanted to forbid the other man to behave in the same way.

Should one, then, not dare to speak about Abraham? I rather think one should. If I had to speak about him, I would begin by portraying the pain of the test. For this purpose I would suck, leech-like, every bit of anxiety and distress and torment out of a father’s suffering, so that I could describe what Abraham suffered while through it all he nevertheless had faith. I would point out that the journey took three days and a good way into the fourth; indeed, those three and a half days should become infinitely longer than the couple of thousand years that separate me from Abraham. Then I would point out — for this is my opinion — that every human being still dares to turn around before he begins on such a thing, and can at any moment turn back in repentance. If this is done, I fear no danger, nor do I fear arousing in people a wish to be put to the proof as Abraham was. But if one wants to sell off a cut-price edition of Abraham, and yet forbid everyone to do the same, then it is ridiculous.

It is now my intention, then, to draw out from the story of Abraham, in the form of problemata — questions set for debate — the dialectical element that lies in it, in order to see what a tremendous paradox faith is: a paradox capable of turning a murder into a holy act, pleasing to God; a paradox that returns Isaac to Abraham, which no thinking can master, because faith begins precisely where thinking leaves off.

chapters.title: Problema I — Is there a teleological suspension of the ethical?
paragraphs: The ethical as such is the universal. As the universal, it applies to everyone — which can also be put another way: it applies at every moment. It rests immanently in itself: nothing outside it is its telos (its end: the purpose it exists for). Instead, it is itself the telos of everything outside it, and once the ethical has taken all of that into itself, it goes no further. Taken in his immediacy — as a being of senses and soul — the single individual is the individual who has his telos in the universal. His ethical task is to express himself in the universal continually: to cancel his particularity (whatever sets him apart as this one person) in order to become the universal. As soon as the single individual tries to assert himself in his particularity against the universal, he sins; the only way back to reconciliation with the universal is to acknowledge that he has sinned. Whenever the single individual, after having entered the universal, feels an urge to assert himself as the single individual, he is in a spiritual trial — an inner assault on him — and he can work his way out of it only by repenting and giving himself up, as the single individual, in the universal. If this is the highest thing that can be said about a human being and his existence, then the ethical has the same character as the eternal blessedness of a human being, which for all eternity and at every moment is his telos. For it would be a contradiction if eternal blessedness could be given up (that is, teleologically suspended). For the moment eternal blessedness was suspended, it would be forfeited — whereas whatever is teleologically suspended is not forfeited, but is preserved precisely in the higher thing that is its telos.

If that is how things stand, then Hegel is right when, at the stage of "the Good and Conscience," he defines a human being only as the single individual. He is right to regard this condition as a "moral form of evil" (see especially his Philosophy of Right), one that must be cancelled in the teleology of ethical life — the ethics lived out in a people's shared customs and institutions. On this view, the single individual who remains at that stage either sins or is in a spiritual trial. Where Hegel is wrong, however, is in speaking of faith. He is wrong not to raise a loud and public protest when Abraham is honored and celebrated as a father of faith, whereas Abraham ought instead to be sent back to a lower court and expelled as a murderer.

For faith is precisely this paradox: that the single individual is higher than the universal. But note carefully how this is so: the movement is repeated. Having first been in the universal, the single individual now isolates himself, as the single individual, as higher than the universal. If faith is not this, then Abraham is lost, and there has never been faith in the world — precisely because there has always been faith. For suppose that the ethical — that is, ethical life — is the highest, and that nothing incommensurable remains in a human being (nothing that cannot be measured by that common standard) except in the sense that this incommensurable element is evil, namely the particular, which ought to be expressed in the universal. In that case one needs no categories beyond those Greek philosophy had, or those that consistent thinking can derive from them. Hegel should not have concealed this; after all, he had studied the Greeks.

One quite often hears men who, instead of losing themselves in study, lose themselves in phrases, announce that a light shines over the Christian world while darkness broods over paganism. This talk has always struck me as strange, since every more thorough thinker, every more serious artist, still renews himself in the eternal youth of the Greek people. Such a statement can be explained by the fact that people do not know what to say, only that they must say something. It is quite in order to say that paganism did not have faith. But if saying so is to mean anything, one must be a little clearer about what one understands by faith; otherwise one sinks back into phrases like these. It is easy to explain the whole of existence, faith included, without having any idea of what faith is. And the man who counts on being admired for such an explanation is not the worst calculator in life; for it is just as Boileau puts it: un sot trouve toujours un plus sot, qui l'admire — a fool always finds a bigger fool to admire him.

Faith is precisely this paradox: that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal — is justified over against it, not subordinate to it but above it. But note carefully how this is so: it is the single individual who, after having been subordinate to the universal as the single individual, now, through the universal, becomes the single individual who as the single individual stands above it — that the single individual as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute. This position cannot be mediated — that is, it cannot be brought under the universal — for all mediation takes place precisely by means of the universal. Now and forever it remains a paradox that thought cannot reach. And yet either faith is this paradox, or else — these are the consequences I ask the reader to keep in mind at every point, even though it would become too long-winded for me to write them out everywhere — or else there has never been faith, precisely because there has always been faith, or else Abraham is lost.

It is true that the single individual can easily mistake this paradox for a spiritual trial, but that is no reason to conceal it. It is true that many people may be so constituted that the paradox repels them. But that is no reason to turn faith into something else so that one can have it too; better to admit that one does not have it. And those who do have faith should take care to set out some marks by which one could tell the paradox apart from a spiritual trial.

Now, the story of Abraham contains just such a teleological suspension of the ethical. There has been no shortage of sharp minds and thorough scholars who have found analogies to it. Their wisdom comes down to the fine principle that basically everything is the same. If one looks a little more closely, I very much doubt that anyone will find a single analogy in the whole world — except a later one, which proves nothing if it stands firm that Abraham represents faith, and that in him faith is expressed as the norm — in a man whose life is not only the most paradoxical that thought can conceive, but so paradoxical that thought cannot conceive it at all. He acts by virtue of the absurd; for the absurd is precisely this: that he as the single individual is higher than the universal. This paradox cannot be mediated. For as soon as Abraham begins to mediate it, he has to admit that he was in a spiritual trial; and if so, he never gets as far as sacrificing Isaac — or, if he has already sacrificed Isaac, he must return in repentance to the universal. By virtue of the absurd he gets Isaac back. Abraham is therefore at no moment a tragic hero; he is something altogether different — either a murderer or a believer. The middle term that saves the tragic hero is something Abraham does not have. That is why I can understand a tragic hero but cannot understand Abraham, even though in a certain mad sense I admire him more than anyone else.

Ethically expressed, Abraham's relation to Isaac is quite simply this: the father must love the son more than himself. But the ethical has several gradations within its own range. We shall see whether this story contains any higher expression of the ethical that could explain his conduct ethically — that could ethically justify him in suspending his ethical obligation to his son, without his thereby going beyond the teleology of the ethical, the ordering of purposes that lies within the ethical itself.

When an undertaking that concerns a whole people is thwarted, when such an enterprise is halted by heaven's disfavor, when the god in his anger sends a windless calm that makes a mockery of all their labor, when the seer carries out his heavy task and announces that the god demands a young girl as a sacrifice — then the father must heroically make this sacrifice. Nobly he must hide his pain, though he might well wish to be "the lowly man who dares to weep" rather than the king whose part is to act royally. And though the pain enters his breast in solitude, and only three people in the nation share his secret, soon the whole nation will share in his pain — but will also share in his deed: that he was willing to offer her up for the common good — her, his daughter, the lovely young girl. "O breast! O fair cheeks, golden hair!" (line 687). The daughter's tears will move him; the father will look away; but it is the hero who will lift the knife. — And when word of it comes back to the land of their fathers, the beautiful girls of Greece will blush with enthusiasm; and if the daughter was a bride, her betrothed will not be angry but proud to share in the father's deed, because the girl belonged to him more tenderly than she belonged to her father.

When the brave judge who saved Israel in its hour of need binds God and himself, in one breath, by the same vow, then he must heroically turn the young girl's jubilation, his beloved daughter's joy, into sorrow, and all Israel will mourn with her for her virgin youth. But every free-born man will understand Jephthah, every stout-hearted woman will admire him, and every virgin in Israel will wish to act as his daughter did. For what good would it have done that Jephthah won the victory through his vow, if he did not keep it? Would the victory not then be taken from the people again?

When a son is forgetful of his duty, when the state puts the judge's sword into the father's hand, when the laws require that the penalty come from the father himself, then the father must heroically forget that the offender is his own son. Nobly he must hide his pain, but there will not be a single person in the nation, not even the son, who does not admire the father. And every time the laws of Rome are interpreted, it will be remembered that many interpreted them more learnedly, but none more gloriously, than Brutus.

But suppose that Agamemnon, while a favorable wind was carrying the fleet under full sail toward its goal, had sent that messenger to fetch Iphigenia in order to sacrifice her. Suppose that Jephthah, without being bound by any vow that decided the fate of the people, had said to his daughter: "Mourn your short youth for two months now, and then I will sacrifice you." Suppose that Brutus had had a righteous son and had still called the lictors to execute him. Who would have understood them? And if these three men, asked why they did it, had answered, "It is a test in which we are being put to the proof" — would anyone have understood them better?

When Agamemnon, Jephthah and Brutus, at the decisive moment, heroically overcome the pain, have heroically lost what they love, and have only to carry out the deed outwardly, then there will never be a noble soul in the world who does not shed tears of sympathy for their pain and tears of admiration for their deed. But suppose that at the decisive moment these three men were to add, to the heroism with which they bore the pain, these few little words: "But it will not happen." Who would understand them then? And if they explained, "We believe this by virtue of the absurd," would that make them any easier to understand? For anyone could readily understand that it was absurd — but who could understand that one could then believe it?

The difference between the tragic hero and Abraham is plain to see. The tragic hero still stays within the ethical. He lets one expression of the ethical have its telos in a higher expression of the ethical. He reduces the ethical relation between father and son, or between daughter and father, to a feeling whose dialectic lies in its relation to the idea of ethical life. So here there can be no question of a teleological suspension of the ethical itself.

With Abraham it is different. By his deed he overstepped the ethical altogether, and he had a higher telos outside it, in relation to which he suspended the ethical. For I would really like to know how anyone would bring Abraham's deed into relation with the universal — whether any connection whatever can be found between what Abraham did and the universal, other than that Abraham transgressed it. Abraham does not do it to save a nation, nor to uphold the idea of the state, nor to appease angry gods. If one could speak of the deity's anger at all, the anger was directed at Abraham alone, and Abraham's entire deed has no relation to the universal; it is a purely private undertaking. So while the tragic hero is great through the virtue of ethical life, Abraham is great through a purely personal virtue. In Abraham's life there is no higher expression of the ethical than this: the father must love the son. The ethical in the sense of ethical life is entirely out of the question here. Insofar as the universal was present at all, it was hidden in Isaac — concealed, so to speak, in Isaac's loins — and would have had to cry out with Isaac's mouth: "Do not do it! You are destroying everything."

What, then, is Abraham's reason? He acts for God's sake and — which is wholly the same thing — for his own. For God's sake, because God requires this proof of his faith; for his own sake, so that he may furnish that proof. The unity of these two is expressed quite correctly in the phrase that has always been used for this situation: it is a test, a temptation. A temptation — but what does that mean? Normally a temptation is something that would keep a person from doing his duty. Here, though, the ethical itself is the temptation: it is what would keep him from doing the will of God. What, then, is duty? Duty is, after all, precisely the expression of God's will.

Here it becomes clear that a new category is needed in order to understand Abraham. Paganism does not know such a relation to the deity. The tragic hero does not enter into any private relation to the deity; the ethical is the divine, and therefore whatever is paradoxical in his situation can be mediated in the universal.

Abraham cannot be mediated; to say the same thing differently, he cannot speak. The moment I speak, I am expressing the universal; and if I do not speak, nobody can understand me. So as soon as Abraham wants to express himself in the universal, he has to say that his situation is a spiritual trial. For no higher expression of the universal — one that stands above the universal he is transgressing — is available to him.

So Abraham fills me with admiration and at the same time with horror. Someone who denies himself and offers himself up to duty gives up the finite in order to grasp the infinite, and he stands on firm enough ground. The tragic hero gives up what is certain for what is still more certain, and the onlooker's eye rests on him with confidence. But the one who gives up the universal to grasp something still higher that is not the universal — what is he doing? Is it possible that this could be anything other than a spiritual trial? And if it is possible, but the single individual grasped wrongly, what salvation is there for him? He suffers all the pain of the tragic hero, he destroys his joy in the world, he renounces everything — and perhaps at the same moment he bars himself from the exalted joy that was so precious to him that he would have bought it at any price. The onlooker cannot understand him at all, nor let his eye rest on him with confidence. Perhaps what the believer intends cannot be done at all, since it is unthinkable. Or if it could be done, but the single individual had misunderstood the deity, what salvation would there be for him then? The tragic hero needs tears and demands tears. And where was the envious eye so barren that it could not weep with Agamemnon? But where was the person whose soul was so lost that he presumed to weep over Abraham? The tragic hero completes his deed at a definite moment in time; but as time goes on he does something no less: he visits the person whose soul is gripped by sorrow, whose chest cannot draw breath for stifled sighs, whose thoughts hang heavy over him, pregnant with tears. He appears to him, breaks the spell of sorrow, loosens the corset, and draws out the tear, as the sufferer forgets his own sufferings in the hero's. Over Abraham no one can weep. One approaches him with a horror religiosus — a holy dread — as Israel approached Mount Sinai. — Think, then, of the solitary man who climbs Mount Moriah, whose peak towers sky-high above the plains of Aulis. Suppose he is not a sleepwalker who walks safely over the abyss while the one who stands at the foot of the mountain, looking up, trembles with anxiety and, out of reverence and dread, does not even dare to call out to him. Suppose he becomes deranged in himself; suppose he had made a mistake! — Thanks, and thanks again, to the man who, when life's sorrows have assaulted someone and left him naked, holds out to him the expression, the fig leaf of the word, to hide his wretchedness! Thanks to you, great Shakespeare, who can put everything — everything, everything — into words exactly as it is — and yet why did you never give voice to this torment? Did you perhaps keep it for yourself, like the beloved whose name one cannot even bear to hear the world speak? For a poet buys this power of the word, the power to speak all the heavy secrets of others, at the price of one little secret he cannot speak; and a poet is no apostle: he drives out devils only with the devil's own power.

But when the ethical has been teleologically suspended in this way, how does the single individual in whom it is suspended exist? He exists as the single individual in opposition to the universal. Does he sin, then? For, seen in terms of the idea (that is, in principle), this is the form of sin. Even a child, who does not sin because it is not conscious of its existence as such, has an existence that, seen in terms of the idea, is sin; and the ethical demands itself of the child at every moment. If one denies that this form — the single individual standing against the universal — can be repeated in such a way that it is not sin, then judgment has been passed on Abraham. How, then, did Abraham exist? He had faith. This is the paradox that keeps him at the summit, the paradox he cannot make clear to anyone else. For the paradox is that he, as the single individual, puts himself in an absolute relation to the absolute. Is he justified? His justification is, once again, something paradoxical; for if he is justified, he is so not by virtue of being something universal but by virtue of being the single individual.

How, then, does the single individual make sure that he is justified? It is easy enough to flatten the whole of existence into the idea of the state or of society. Do that, and one can also mediate easily enough; for then one never arrives at the paradox that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal — which I can also express pointedly with a saying of Pythagoras: that the odd number is more perfect than the even. When, now and then in our time, one does hear an answer that points in the direction of the paradox, it usually runs like this: "It must be judged by the outcome." A hero who has become a skandalon — a stumbling block, an offense — to his contemporaries, conscious that he is a paradox who cannot make himself understood, calls out confidently to his age: "The outcome will surely prove that I was justified." In our time one hears this cry more rarely; for just as our age does not produce heroes, which is its failing, it has the advantage that it produces few caricatures either. So when in our time one hears the words "It must be judged by the outcome," one knows at once whom one has the honor of addressing. Those who talk this way are a numerous tribe, which I will call by the common name of the lecturers. In their thoughts they live secure in existence: they have a fixed position and safe prospects in a well-organized state; they have centuries, perhaps even millennia, between themselves and the upheavals of existence; they have no fear that such things could happen again — what would the police and the newspapers say? Their work in life is to judge the great men, and to judge them by the outcome. Such conduct toward greatness betrays a strange mixture of arrogance and wretchedness: arrogance, because they think themselves called to judge; wretchedness, because they do not feel their own lives to be even remotely related to those of the great. Anyone with even a little erectioris ingenii — a more elevated cast of mind — has not become an entirely cold and clammy mollusk; and as he approaches what is great, he can never forget that since the creation of the world it has been the custom for the outcome to come last, and that anyone who really means to learn from greatness must look precisely at how it began. Whoever is to act and wants to judge himself by the outcome will never begin. Even if the outcome delights the whole world, it cannot help the hero; for he learned the outcome only when the whole thing was over, and it was not by the outcome that he became a hero — he was one because he began.

Besides, the outcome (insofar as it is finitude's answer to the infinite question) is, in its dialectic, entirely different in kind from the hero's existence. Or is the fact that Abraham received Isaac by a miracle supposed to prove that Abraham was justified in relating himself as the single individual to the universal? If Abraham had actually sacrificed Isaac, would he have been any less justified?

But people are curious about the outcome, as they are about how a book ends. The anxiety, the distress, the paradox — of these they want to know nothing. They flirt aesthetically with the outcome; it arrives just as unexpectedly, but also just as easily, as a lottery prize; and once they have heard the outcome, they feel edified. And yet no temple robber laboring in chains and irons is so base a criminal as the one who plunders the holy in this way; and Judas himself, who sold his master for thirty pieces of silver, is no more despicable than the one who puts greatness up for sale like this.

It goes against my soul to speak inhumanly about greatness — to let it loom dimly, in vague outline, at an enormous distance; to let it be great without bringing out what is human in it, and so it stops being great. What makes me great is not what befalls me but what I do; and surely no one thinks a man became great because he won the big prize in the lottery. Even if a person was born in humble circumstances, I still require of him that he not be so inhuman toward himself that he can think of the king's castle only from a distance, dreaming vaguely of its greatness, at once wanting to exalt it and to cancel it by exalting it in a servile way. I require of him that he be human enough to step forward there too, with confidence and dignity. He must not be so inhuman as to want to violate everything impudently by storming straight in from the street into the king's halls; by doing so he loses more than the king does. Rather, it should please him to keep every rule of good manners, with a happy, trusting eagerness that is exactly what will give him his freedom and boldness. This is only an image, for that difference in rank is a very imperfect expression of distance in the world of spirit. I require of every human being that he not think of himself so inhumanly as not to dare to go into those palaces where not only the memory of the chosen lives but where the chosen themselves live. He should not push forward impudently and force his kinship on them. He should be blessed every time he bows before them, but he should be bold and confident, and always something more than a charwoman — for if he refuses to be anything more, he will never get in. What will help him is exactly the anxiety and distress through which the great are put to the proof; for otherwise, if he has any backbone at all, the great would only arouse his justified envy. And whatever can be great only at a distance, whatever people try to make great with empty and hollow phrases — people themselves destroy it.

Who in all the world was ever as great as that woman who found favor, the Mother of God, the Virgin Mary? Yet how do people talk about it? Being the favored one among women is not what makes her great. And if it did not so strangely happen that those who listen can think just as inhumanly as those who speak, then surely every young girl would ask: "Why was I not the favored one too?" And if I had nothing else to say, I would certainly not dismiss such a question as stupid; for when it comes to a favor, seen abstractly, every human being has an equal claim. What people leave out is the distress, the anxiety, the paradox. My thought is as pure as anyone's, and whoever can think such things will surely find his thought becoming pure; and if it does not, he has something terrible to expect. For whoever has once called up these images cannot get rid of them again. And if he sins against them, they take revenge terribly, with a silent wrath more terrible than the loud clamor of ten ravening reviewers. Mary did bear the child miraculously, but it went with her as it goes with women, and that time is a time of anxiety, distress and paradox. The angel was a ministering spirit, certainly — but not an obliging spirit that went round to the other young girls in Israel saying, "Do not despise Mary; something extraordinary is happening to her." The angel came only to Mary, and no one could understand her. What woman was ever so wronged as Mary? And does it not hold here too that whom God blesses, he curses in the same breath? This is how the spirit understands Mary. And she is by no means — it outrages me to say it, but it outrages me even more that people have thoughtlessly and frivolously thought of her this way — she is by no means a fine lady sitting in state and playing with a divine child. When she nevertheless said, "Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord," then she is great, and it should not be hard, I think, to explain why she became the Mother of God. She has no need of the world's admiration, just as Abraham has no need of tears; she was not a heroine, nor he a hero. Yet both became greater than heroes — not at all by being spared the distress, the torment and the paradox, but through them.

There is greatness in a poet who sets his tragic hero before the public to be admired and ventures to say: "Weep for him, he is worthy of it." To be worthy of the tears of those who are worthy to weep is a great thing. There is greatness in the poet's daring to keep the crowd in its place and to take people to task, so that each one examines himself to see whether he is worthy to weep over the hero; for the waste water of blubberers degrades what is holy. — But greater than all this is that the knight of faith dares to say even to the noble person who wants to weep over him: "Do not weep for me, but weep for yourself."

People are moved; they long to go back to those beautiful times; sweet, tender longings lead them to the goal of their wish — to see Christ walking about in the promised land. They forget the anxiety, the distress, the paradox. Was it such an easy matter not to be mistaken? Was it not terrifying that this human being walking among the others was God, terrifying to share a meal with him? Was becoming an apostle such a simple thing? But the outcome, eighteen centuries, helps — it helps with this shabby deception by which people deceive themselves and others. I do not feel courageous enough to wish I had been contemporary with such events; but for that reason I do not judge harshly those who were mistaken, nor think little of those who saw what was right.
But I return to Abraham. In the time before the outcome, either Abraham was a murderer every minute, or we stand before the paradox that is higher than all mediations.

The story of Abraham, then, contains a teleological suspension of the ethical. As the single individual, he has become higher than the universal. This is the paradox that cannot be mediated. It is just as inexplicable how he entered it as how he remains in it. If this is not how things stand with Abraham, then he is not even a tragic hero but a murderer. To go on calling him the father of faith, to talk about this to people who care about nothing but words, is thoughtless. A human being can become a tragic hero by his own strength, but not a knight of faith. When someone sets out on the tragic hero's road — hard, in a certain sense — many will be able to advise him; but the one who walks the narrow road of faith no one can advise, no one can understand. Faith is a miracle, and yet no human being is excluded from it; for what unites all human life is passion, and faith is a passion.

chapters.title: Problema II — Is there an absolute duty to God?
paragraphs: The ethical is the universal, and as such it is also the divine. So it is right to say that every duty is at bottom a duty to God. But if one can say no more than that, then one is also saying that I really have no duty to God. What makes a duty a duty is that it is traced back to God; yet within the duty itself I stand in no relation to God. Loving one's neighbor, for instance, is a duty. It is a duty because it is traced back to God; but in this duty I enter into a relation not with God but with the neighbor I love. If I then say, in this context, that it is my duty to love God, I am really saying only a tautology — the same thing twice — insofar as "God" is here taken in a wholly abstract sense as the divine, that is, the universal, that is, duty. Then the entire existence of humankind is rounded off in itself as a perfect sphere, and the ethical is at once what bounds it and what fills it. God shrinks to an invisible, vanishing point, a thought without power; whatever power he has lies in the ethical, which fills existence. So if anyone should take it into his head to love God in any sense other than the one just stated, he is overwrought: he loves a phantom which, if it only had strength enough to speak, would tell him, "I do not require your love — just stay where you belong." If anyone should take it into his head to love God in some other way, this love becomes suspect, like the love Rousseau speaks of, with which a person loves a distant African people instead of loving his neighbor.

Now, if what has been set out here is correct — if there is nothing incommensurable in a human life, and whatever incommensurable there is exists only by accident, from which nothing follows insofar as existence is viewed in terms of the idea — then Hegel is right. But where he is not right is in speaking of faith, or in allowing Abraham to be regarded as its father; for by the second he has pronounced judgment on both Abraham and faith. In Hegel's philosophy, das Äussere (die Entäusserung) — the outer (the act of outwardly expressing oneself) — is higher than das Innere, the inner. This is often illustrated with an example. The child is das Innere, the inner; the man is das Äussere, the outer. That is why the child is determined precisely by what is outer — and why, conversely, the man, being das Äussere, is determined precisely by das Innere. Faith, however, is this paradox: that inwardness is higher than outwardness — or, to recall an expression used earlier, that the odd number is higher than the even.

For the ethical view of life, then, the task of the single individual is to strip himself of the determination of inwardness and to express it in something outward. Every time the single individual shrinks from this, every time he wants to hold back in, or slip back into, the inward determinations of feeling, mood and so on, he sins; he is in a spiritual trial. The paradox of faith is this: that there is an inwardness that is incommensurable with the outward — an inwardness which, note carefully, is not identical with the first inwardness but is a new inwardness. This point must not be missed. Recent philosophy has taken the liberty of simply putting "the immediate" — what is simply there before any reflection — in the place of "faith." Once that is done, it would be ridiculous to deny that there has been faith in every age. Faith then keeps rather ordinary company: feeling, mood, idiosyncrasy, vapeurs (fits of the vapors) and the like. To that extent philosophy may have a point when it says one should not remain there. But philosophy has no warrant for using the word that way. Faith is preceded by a movement of infinity; only then does faith appear, nec opinate — unexpectedly — by virtue of the absurd. This I can well understand, without thereby claiming that I have faith. If faith is nothing more than what philosophy passes it off as, then Socrates had already gone beyond it, far beyond it — and it is not, the other way round, that he fell short of it. Intellectually, he made the movement of infinity; his ignorance is infinite resignation. This task is already one suited to human powers, even if our age disdains it. But only when it has been done, only when the single individual has exhausted himself in the infinite, only then is there a point at which faith can break forth.

The paradox of faith, then, is this: that the single individual is higher than the universal; that the single individual — to recall a distinction from dogmatics now less often heard — lets his relation to the absolute decide his relation to the universal, rather than letting his relation to the universal decide his relation to the absolute. The paradox can also be put this way: there is an absolute duty to God. For in this relation of duty the single individual, as the single individual, relates himself absolutely to the absolute. So when it is said in this connection that it is a duty to love God, something different is being said from before. For if that duty is absolute, the ethical is brought down to the level of the relative. That does not mean the ethical is to be abolished; rather, it receives an entirely different expression, the paradoxical expression — so that, for example, love for God can lead the knight of faith to give his love for his neighbor an expression that is the opposite of what, ethically speaking, is his duty.
If this is not so, then faith has no place in existence; then faith is a spiritual trial, and Abraham is lost, since he gave in to it.

This paradox cannot be mediated, for it rests precisely on the single individual's being only the single individual. As soon as this single individual wants to express his absolute duty in the universal and become conscious of it there, he recognizes that he is in a spiritual trial. And then, if he does resist the spiritual trial, he will not come to fulfill the so-called absolute duty; and if he does not resist it, he sins, even if in reality his deed turns out to be what was his absolute duty. So what was Abraham to do? If he had said to another person, "Isaac I love above everything in the world, and that is why it weighs so heavily on me to sacrifice him," the other would surely have shaken his head and said, "Then why sacrifice him?" Or, if the other had been a shrewd fellow, he might even have seen through Abraham and noticed that he was displaying feelings that flagrantly contradicted his deed.

In the story of Abraham we find just such a paradox. Ethically expressed, his relation to Isaac is this: the father must love the son. This ethical relation is reduced to the relative, in contrast to the absolute relation to God. Asked why, Abraham can answer only that it is a test, a temptation — which, as noted above, is the unity of its being for God's sake and for his own sake. These two descriptions are linked in ordinary speech as well: when we see someone do something that does not fit into the universal, we say, "He hardly did that for God's sake," and by this we mean that he did it for his own sake. The paradox of faith has lost the middle term, that is, the universal. On the one side it has the expression of the most extreme egoism (doing the terrible thing it does for one's own sake); on the other, the expression of the most absolute devotion (acting for God's sake). Faith as such cannot be mediated into the universal, because that would cancel it. Faith is this paradox, and the single individual simply cannot make himself understood by anyone. People no doubt imagine that the single individual can make himself understood by another single individual who is in the same position. Such a view would be unthinkable if people in our time were not trying in so many ways to sneak slyly into greatness. One knight of faith cannot help another at all. Either the single individual becomes a knight of faith himself, by taking the paradox upon himself, or he never becomes one. Partnership in these regions is utterly unthinkable. Any closer explanation of what is to be understood by "Isaac" is one the single individual can give only to himself. And even if one could define ever so exactly, in general terms, what is to be understood by "Isaac" (which, incidentally, would be the most ridiculous self-contradiction: bringing the single individual, who stands precisely outside the universal, under universal definitions, when he is supposed to act precisely as the single individual who is outside the universal), the single individual could still never be assured of it by others, only by himself as the single individual. So even if a person were cowardly and wretched enough to want to become a knight of faith on someone else's responsibility, he would not become one; for only the single individual becomes one, as the single individual. And that is what is great — which I can understand without entering into it, since I lack the courage. But it is also what is terrible — which I can grasp even better.

As is well known, Luke 14:26 sets out a remarkable teaching about the absolute duty to God: "Whoever comes to me without hating father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters — even his own soul — cannot be my disciple." These are hard words; who can stand to listen to them? And so they are seldom heard. But this silence is only an evasion, and it does no good. The student of theology, meanwhile, learns that these words occur in the New Testament, and in some exegetical handbook he finds the information that μισεῖν (to hate), in this and a few other passages, is used per μείωσιν — by understatement — and means minus diligo, posthabeo, non colo, nihili facio: I love less, I put in second place, I do not honor, I count as nothing. The context in which these words occur, however, does not seem to support this tasteful explanation. For the very next verse tells how someone who wants to build a tower first calculates whether he is able to finish it, so that people will not laugh at him afterward. The close connection between this story and the verse quoted seems to indicate precisely that the words are to be taken as terribly as possible, so that each person may examine himself to see whether he can put up the building.

Suppose that pious and tender-minded exegete, who thinks he can smuggle Christianity into the world by haggling it down in this way, managed to convince someone that this was — grammatically, linguistically and κατ' ἀναλογίαν (by analogy with other passages) — the meaning of that passage. Then he will hopefully also manage, in the same moment, to convince that same person that Christianity is one of the most pitiful things in the world. For think of a doctrine that, at one of its most lyrical moments, when its sense of its own eternal validity is at its fullest, has nothing to say but a noisy word that means nothing and indicates only that one should be less kind, less attentive, more indifferent; a teaching that, at the very moment it makes as if to say something terrible, ends by soothing instead of terrifying — that teaching is surely not worth standing up for.

The words are terrible, yet I do believe they can be understood — without it following that whoever has understood them therefore has the courage to do what they say. One should at least be honest enough to acknowledge what is written there, and to admit that it is great, even if one lacks the courage for it oneself. Whoever behaves this way should not shut himself out from a share in that beautiful story; for in a way it contains comfort even for the one who did not have the courage to begin building the tower. He must be honest, though, and not dress up this want of courage as humility; it is really pride, while the courage of faith is the one courage that is humble.

It is easy to see now that if the passage is to make any sense, it must be understood literally. God is the one who demands absolute love. Now, anyone who demands a person's love and thinks that this love should also prove itself by the person's becoming lukewarm toward everything else he held dear is not only an egoist but also stupid. And whoever demanded such a love would at the same moment be signing his own death sentence, insofar as his life lay in the love he desired. A husband, for instance, requires that his wife leave her father and mother. Yet if he took it as proof of her exceptional love for him that for his sake she became a lukewarm, listless daughter, and so on, then he is stupider than the stupidest. Had he any notion of what love is, he would hope to find that as a daughter and as a sister she loved perfectly. In that he would see a guarantee that his wife would love him as no one else in the kingdom does. So: what one would regard in a human being as a sign of egoism and stupidity — that, with the help of an exegete, one is supposed to regard as a worthy conception of the deity.

But how, then, is one to hate them? I will not bring up here the human distinction "either love or hate" — not because I have much against it, for it is at least passionate, but because it is egoistic and does not fit here. But if I take the task to be a paradox, then I do understand it — understand it, that is, in the only way a paradox can be understood. The absolute duty can then lead one to do what ethics would forbid, but it can by no means lead the knight of faith to stop loving. Abraham shows this. In the moment when he means to sacrifice Isaac, the ethical expression of his act is: he hates Isaac. Yet if he truly hated Isaac, he could be sure that God was not asking this of him; for Cain and Abraham are not the same. Isaac he must love with his whole soul. When God demands Isaac, Abraham must love him, if possible, even more — and only then can he sacrifice him. For it is precisely this love for Isaac that, by its paradoxical opposition to his love for God, makes his deed a sacrifice. But the distress and anxiety in the paradox is that, humanly speaking, he cannot make himself understood at all. Only at the moment when his deed is in absolute contradiction to his feeling does he sacrifice Isaac. But the reality of his deed is what makes him belong to the universal, and there he is and remains a murderer.

The passage in Luke must further be understood in such a way that one sees that the knight of faith has no higher expression of the universal (as the ethical) in which he could save himself. If, for example, the Church were to demand this sacrifice of one of its members, we would have only a tragic hero. For as long as the single individual can get into the Church by a simple mediation, the idea of the Church is not qualitatively distinct from that of the state. And as soon as the single individual has entered the paradox, the idea of the Church is out of his reach; he cannot leave the paradox, and in it he must find either his blessedness or his perdition. Such an ecclesiastical hero — the member of whom the Church demands this sacrifice — expresses the universal in his deed, and everyone in the Church will understand him, down to his own father and mother and the rest. But he is not a knight of faith, and he also gives a different answer from Abraham's: he does not say that it is a test or a temptation in which he is being put to the proof.

People generally refrain from quoting passages like this one in Luke. They are afraid of letting people loose; they fear the worst will happen once the single individual takes it into his head to behave as the single individual. Moreover, people think that existing as the single individual is the easiest thing of all, and that this is exactly why people must be forced to become the universal. I share neither the fear nor the opinion, and my reason is the same in both cases. Whoever has learned that existing as the single individual is the most terrible thing of all should not be afraid to say that it is the greatest. But he must also say it in such a way that his words are unlikely to become a snare for someone who has gone astray, but rather help him into the universal — even if his words make a little room for what is great. If someone dares not speak of such passages, he dares not speak of Abraham either. And to think that existing as the single individual is easy enough contains a very dubious indirect admission about oneself. For whoever really has self-respect and concern for his soul is certain that a person who lives with no overseer but himself, alone in the whole world, lives more strictly and more chastely than a young girl in her chamber. It is true that there may be those who need compulsion — those who, if they were set free, would romp like unruly animals in selfish pleasure. But one must show that one is not one of them precisely by knowing how to speak with anxiety and trembling. And one should speak out of reverence for what is great, so that it is not forgotten out of fear of harm — harm that will surely not come if one speaks in such a way that one knows it is the great, knows its terrors; and without knowing those, one does not know its greatness either.

Let us now consider the distress and anxiety in the paradox of faith a little more closely. The tragic hero renounces himself in order to express the universal; the knight of faith renounces the universal in order to become the single individual. As was said, everything depends on how one is placed. Whoever thinks it is easy enough to be the single individual can always be sure that he is not a knight of faith; for drifters and vagabond geniuses are not men of faith. The knight of faith, by contrast, knows how splendid it is to belong to the universal. He knows how fine and wholesome it is to be the single individual who translates himself into the universal — who, so to speak, himself produces a clean, elegant and as far as possible error-free edition of himself, legible to all. He knows the relief of becoming intelligible to himself in the universal, so that he understands it and every single individual who understands him understands the universal through him, the two of them glad in the safety the universal gives. He knows how good it is to be born as the single individual who has his home in the universal, his friendly dwelling place, which at once receives him with open arms whenever he wants to stay in it. But he also knows that higher up than this there winds a lonely path, narrow and steep. He knows it is terrible to be born in solitude out of the universal, to travel on without once meeting a fellow traveler. He knows perfectly well where he is and where he stands with other people. Humanly speaking, he is mad and cannot make himself understood by anyone. And yet "mad" is the mildest expression. If he is not regarded that way, then he is a hypocrite — and the higher he climbs on that path, the more dreadful a hypocrite he is.

The knight of faith knows that it is inspiring to give oneself up for the universal, that it takes courage, but also that it is safe, precisely because it is done for the universal. He knows how splendid it is to be understood by every noble mind, and in such a way that whoever watches is ennobled by it. He knows this, and it holds him as if with a bond; he could wish that this had been the task assigned to him. So Abraham might now and then have wished that the task were to love Isaac as befits a father, understandably to all, memorably for all time; he could wish that the task were to sacrifice Isaac for the universal, so that he could inspire fathers to glorious deeds. And he is almost horrified at the thought that for him such wishes are only spiritual trials and must be treated as such; for he knows that it is a lonely path he walks, and that he accomplishes nothing for the universal but is himself only put to the proof and tested. Or what did Abraham ever achieve for the universal? Let me talk about it in human terms — thoroughly human terms! He spends seventy years getting a son in his old age. What others get quickly enough and enjoy for a long time takes him seventy years. And why? Because he is being tested and tempted. Is that not madness? But Abraham had faith. It was only Sarah who faltered and persuaded him to take Hagar as a second wife — and for that very reason he had to send Hagar away. He gets Isaac — and then he is to be tested again. He knew it is glorious to express the universal, glorious to live with Isaac. But that is not the task. He knew it would be kingly to sacrifice such a son for the universal; there he would have found rest, and everyone would have rested in praise of his deed, as a vowel rests in the silent letter that carries it. But that is not the task — he is being tested. That Roman general who is famous for his surname Cunctator, "the Delayer," stopped the enemy by delaying — but what a delayer Abraham is compared with him! Yet Abraham does not save the state. This is the content of 130 years. Who can bear it? Would his contemporaries — if one could speak of his having any — not say: "With Abraham it is an eternal delaying. At long last he has a son — and how long it took! — and now he means to sacrifice him. Has he lost his mind? If only he could at least explain why he wants to do it; but it is always 'a test.'" Nor could Abraham explain any more than that; for his life is like a book that has been placed under divine seizure and never becomes publici juris — public property.

This is what is terrible. Whoever does not see it can always be sure that he is no knight of faith. But whoever does see it will not want to deny that even the tragic hero most severely put to the proof moves as if in a dance compared with the knight of faith, who makes his way forward only slowly, crawling. And when he has seen this and has made sure that he lacks the courage to understand it, he will surely have some sense of the wondrous glory that knight attains: that he becomes God's confidant, the Lord's friend, and — to speak quite humanly — that he says "you" to God in heaven, as one speaks to an intimate, while even the tragic hero addresses him only in the third person.

The tragic hero is soon finished, and his struggle is soon over. He makes the infinite movement, and from then on he is safe in the universal. The knight of faith, on the other hand, is kept sleepless; for he is constantly being tested, and at every moment there is the possibility of turning back in repentance to the universal — and this possibility can just as well be a spiritual trial as the truth. He cannot get clarity about this from any human being; for then he would be outside the paradox.

The knight of faith, then, has first and foremost the passion to concentrate into a single moment the whole of the ethical that he is breaking, so that he can give himself the assurance that he truly loves Isaac with all his soul. If he cannot, he is in a spiritual trial. Next, he has the passion to call up this whole assurance in an instant, and in such a way that it is just as fully valid as it was in the first moment. If he cannot do that, he gets nowhere; for then he must keep starting over from the beginning. The tragic hero also concentrates into one moment the ethical that he teleologically went beyond, but in this respect he has support in the universal. The knight of faith has only himself alone, and that is what is terrible. Most people live under ethical obligation by letting each day bring its own sorrow; but then they never arrive at this passionate concentration, this energetic consciousness. In a certain sense the universal can help the tragic hero attain it, but the knight of faith is alone in everything. The tragic hero does it and finds rest in the universal; the knight of faith is kept in constant tension. Agamemnon gives up Iphigenia and has thereby found rest in the universal; now he proceeds to sacrifice her. If Agamemnon has not made the movement — if at the decisive moment his soul, instead of passionate concentration, was lost in the common chatter about having several daughters and about how vielleicht das Ausserordentliche (perhaps the extraordinary) might still happen — then of course he is no hero but a case for the poorhouse. Abraham has the hero's concentration too, though in him it is far more difficult, since he has no support at all in the universal; but he goes on to make a further movement, in which he gathers his soul back and fixes it on the miracle. If Abraham has not done that, he is only an Agamemnon — assuming one could even explain how it can be justified to want to sacrifice Isaac when doing so benefits the universal in no way.

Whether the single individual is really in a spiritual trial or is a knight of faith, only the single individual himself can decide. Nevertheless, some marks can be constructed from the paradox that even someone who is not in it can understand. The true knight of faith is always absolute isolation; the false knight is sectarian. Sectarianism is an attempt to jump off the narrow way of the paradox and become a tragic hero at a bargain price. The tragic hero expresses the universal and sacrifices himself for it. Instead of this, the sectarian Master Jackel — a puppet-show clown — keeps a private theater: a handful of good friends and fellows who stand for the universal roughly as well as the court witnesses in The Gold Snuffbox represent justice. The knight of faith, on the contrary, is the paradox; he is the single individual, absolutely nothing but the single individual, without any connections or complications. This is the terrible thing that the sectarian weakling cannot endure. For instead of learning from it that he is unable to do what is great, and then plainly admitting it — something I naturally cannot but approve of, since it is what I do myself — the bungler thinks that by joining forces with a few other bunglers he will be able to do it. But that will not work at all; in the world of spirit no cheating is tolerated. A dozen sectarians go arm in arm; they know nothing at all of the lonely spiritual trials that await the knight of faith and that he dares not flee, precisely because it would be still more terrible if he presumptuously forced his way forward. The sectarians drown one another out with noise and clamor and keep anxiety away with their shouting; and a hooting fairground crowd like this thinks it is storming heaven and thinks it is walking the same path as the knight of faith — who, in the solitude of the universe, never hears a human voice but walks alone with his terrible responsibility.

The knight of faith is thrown back on himself alone. He feels the pain of not being able to make himself understood by others, but he has no vain desire to guide anyone else. The pain is what assures him. The vain desire he does not know; his soul is too earnest for that. The false knight easily betrays himself by the mastery he has acquired in an instant. He does not grasp at all what is at issue: that if another single individual is to walk the same path, he must become the single individual in exactly the same way, and then he needs no one's guidance — least of all that of someone who wants to force himself on him. Here, again, people jump off the path: they cannot endure the martyrdom of being uncomprehended, and instead, conveniently enough, they choose the worldly admiration that mastery brings. The true knight of faith is a witness, never a teacher, and in this lies the deep humanity that is worth rather more than the silly concern for other people's weal and woe that is honored under the name of sympathy, though it is nothing but vanity. Whoever wants only to be a witness thereby confesses that no human being, not even the lowliest, needs another's sympathy or should be humbled by it so that the other can be raised up. But just as he did not win what he won on the cheap, he does not sell it cheap either. He is not base enough to accept people's admiration and pay them for it with his silent contempt. He knows that true greatness is open to everyone alike.

So either there is an absolute duty to God — and if there is, it is the paradox described here: that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal and as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute — or there has never been faith, because there has always been faith; or Abraham is lost; or one must explain the passage in Luke 14 as that tasteful exegete did, and explain the corresponding passages, and similar ones, in the same way.

chapters.title: Problema III — Was it ethically defensible for Abraham to keep silent about his undertaking to Sarah, to Eliezer and to Isaac?
paragraphs: The ethical as such is the universal, and, as the universal, it is in turn what is disclosed. Taken in his immediacy — as a being of senses and soul — the single individual is the concealed one. His ethical task, then, is to work himself free of his concealment — his state of being hidden — and to become disclosed in the universal. So every time he wants to remain in concealment, he sins and is in a spiritual trial, and he can come out of it only by disclosing himself.

Here we stand once again at the same point. If there is no concealment that has its ground in this — that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal — then Abraham’s conduct cannot be defended; for he passed over the intermediate ethical authorities. If, on the other hand, there is such a concealment, then we stand before the paradox, which cannot be mediated, since it rests precisely on the single individual’s being, as the single individual, higher than the universal — but the universal is precisely mediation. The Hegelian philosophy assumes no justified concealment, no justified incommensurability. It is therefore consistent with itself when it demands disclosure — that the individual bring what is hidden in him out into the open, and make himself known. But it is confused when it wants to regard Abraham as the father of faith and to talk about faith. For faith is not the first immediacy but a later one. The first immediacy is the aesthetic, and here the Hegelian philosophy may well be right. But faith is not the aesthetic — or else there has never been faith, because there has always been faith.

The best course here will be to consider the whole matter purely aesthetically, and to that end to enter into an aesthetic deliberation. I would ask the reader to give himself over to it completely for the time being, while I, to do my part, will adapt my presentation to its subjects. The category I want to consider a little more closely is the interesting — what stands at a crisis, where things hang in the balance. It is a category that has gained great importance, especially in our time, precisely because the age lives in discrimine rerum — at a turning point in affairs; for it is really the category of the turning point. So one should not, as sometimes happens, first love it oneself pro virili — to the best of one’s powers — and then scorn it because it has grown beyond one. But neither should one be all too greedy for it. For this much is certain: to become interesting, or to have an interesting life, is not a task for artful industry but a fateful privilege, which can be bought only at the price of deep pain, as can every privilege in the world of spirit. Thus Socrates was the most interesting human being who has ever lived, and his life the most interesting ever led; but this existence was assigned to him by the god, and insofar as he had to acquire it himself, he was no stranger to toil and pain either. To want to take such an existence in vain is unbecoming for anyone who thinks at all seriously about life; and yet in our time one not infrequently sees examples of such striving. The interesting, moreover, is a border category, a confinium — a borderland — between aesthetics and ethics. To that extent the deliberation must constantly stray over into the territory of ethics, while, if it is to have any significance, it must seize the problem with aesthetic inwardness and concupiscence. In our time ethics seldom engages in such things. The reason is said to be that there can be no room for them in the System. Well then, one could do it in monographs. And besides, if one does not want to be long-winded about it, one can do it briefly and still achieve the same thing — provided, that is, that one has the predicate in one’s power; for one or two predicates can betray a whole world. Is there to be no room in the System for such little words either?

Aristotle says in his immortal Poetics: δύο μὲν οὖν τοῦ μύθου μέρη, περὶ ταῦτ’ ἐστί, περιπέτεια καὶ ἀναγνώρισις — two parts of the plot, then, turn on these things: peripeteia, the reversal, and anagnorisis, the recognition (cf. chapter 11). Naturally it is only the second element that concerns me here: ἀναγνώρισις, recognition. Wherever there can be talk of a recognition, there is eo ipso — by that very fact — talk of a preceding concealment. Just as the recognition is what resolves, what releases the tension, so the concealment is what builds the suspense, the tension, in dramatic life. Earlier in the same chapter Aristotle develops the differing worth of tragedies according to how περιπέτεια and ἀναγνώρισις carom off each other, and discusses single and double recognition. I cannot take account of that here, however much it tempts by its inwardness and its quiet absorption — especially someone who has long enough been wearied by the superficial omniscience of the survey-writers. A more general remark must find its place here. In Greek tragedy, concealment (and, as a consequence, recognition) is an epic remnant. It has its ground in a fate in which the dramatic action vanishes, and from which that action has its dark, enigmatic origin. That is why the effect a Greek tragedy produces resembles the impression a marble statue makes, lacking as it does the power of the eye. Greek tragedy is blind. That is why a certain abstraction is required in order to be properly affected by it. A son murders his father, but only afterward does he learn that it was his father. A sister is about to sacrifice her brother, but at the decisive moment she finds out. This kind of tragedy can have less hold on our reflective age. Modern drama has given up fate; it has emancipated itself dramatically; it is sighted; it gazes into itself and takes fate up into its dramatic consciousness. Concealment and disclosure are then the hero’s free act, for which he is responsible.

In modern drama, too, recognition and concealment belong as an essential element. To cite examples of this would be too long-winded. I am polite enough to assume that anyone in our time who is so aesthetically voluptuous, so potent and so inflamed that he conceives as easily as the partridge, which, according to Aristotle, needs only to hear the cock’s voice or his flight over her head — I assume that anyone, merely on hearing the word “concealment,” will easily be able to shake ten or so novels and comedies out of his sleeve. I can therefore be brief and so straight away merely indicate a more general remark. If the one who plays hide-and-seek, and thereby brings dramatic ferment into the play, is hiding some nonsense, we get a comedy; if, however, he stands in relation to the idea, he can come close to being a tragic hero. Here is just one example of the comic. A man wears makeup and a wig. This same man would dearly like to make a conquest of the fair sex, and he is quite sure of victory with the help of the makeup and the wig, which render him unconditionally irresistible. He catches a girl and stands on the summit of happiness. Now comes the catch. Can he confess it? Will he not lose all his bewitching power when he shows himself as a plain, ordinary — indeed, even a bald — male person? Will he not thereby lose his beloved again? — His concealment is his free act, for which aesthetics, too, holds him responsible. This science is no friend of bald hypocrites; it hands him over to laughter. This must be enough merely to indicate what I mean; the comic cannot be the object of this investigation’s interest.
